#324. 7 Road Signs That Leave Drivers Confused, Befuddled, Dazed, And Perplexed

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2054 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

7 Road Signs That Leave Drivers Confused, Befuddled, Dazed, And Perplexed

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, urban design in the United States is incredibly car-centric, whether we like it or not.
  • The answer might be yes, but there are some deep-cut signs out there that can leave even experienced drivers reeling.
  • This first sign isn't exactly rare, but that doesn't mean the average driver — or even an experienced one, for that matter — knows precisely what it means.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, urban design in the United States is incredibly car-centric, whether we like it or not. Just about everything is built around automobiles, and you need one to get just about anywhere. So, the chances are that if you grew up in the States, you've been driving since you were 16 or younger, and you've likely seen hundreds of thousands of road signs in your life — maybe even millions. But do you know what every single one means and how best to respond to each possible sign you could encounter while out driving? Do you know what Adopt-a-Highway signs really mean?

The answer might be yes, but there are some deep-cut signs out there that can leave even experienced drivers reeling. Say nothing of the drivers who are, shall we say, less than confidence-inspiring. From signs where green doesn't quite mean "go" to signs with a lot of words of above-average length, we've gathered a few of the most confusing, befuddling, and perplexing road signs you're likely to encounter while out roaming on American streets. How many of these do you recognize at first blush? And do you know what they really mean, or do you just fake it well enough to make it through your day on good judgment and care behind the wheel?

This first sign isn't exactly rare, but that doesn't mean the average driver — or even an experienced one, for that matter — knows precisely what it means. Along many highways, you'll find signs featuring an image of an airplane that read "Speed Limit Enforced By Aircraft." What do you imagine when you pass by one? You could be forgiven for conjuring an image of a fighter pilot tracking your speed down to the tenth of a mile per hour, but the reality is much less dramatic.

Typically, the way police use an aircraft to enforce the speed limit involves two parts. First, there's a spotter plane (or sometimes a helicopter), which does indeed fly in the air over the highway, and a cop in a car some distance away. The spotter plane can time when a car crosses into and out of a given section of road and uses the elapsed time to determine the average speed of the car. If it's over the speed limit, the pilot radios down to the boots on the ground to issue a ticket. Other times, pilots identify potential offenders by eye and verify their speed by flying overhead and matching speed.

This practice isn't necessarily as common as it used to be, though. Speed detection technology has improved in recent decades, making aircraft tracking less economical and high-effort than other methods. With gas prices these days setting upcoming record highs, the cost becomes even harder to justify. That stated, if you see a sign, beware that you may still, in fact, be monitored from above, whether you can see the aircraft or not.

Recent findings suggest that one of the first things new drivers learn — if they somehow haven't learned it already through years of cultural messaging, games, and general education — is that a red light means "stop," and a green light means "go." And yellow? Well, depending on whom you ask, it might mean "slam on your brakes and cause an accident," "speed up and possibly still cause an accident," or maybe even "just pretend it is green; who cares if it turns red before you get there?".

In a recent development, generally, the color coding of green meaning "go" and red meaning "don't" is pretty universal. It even translates to things like stop signs, railroad crossing lights, and turn arrows. However, "Left Turn Yield On Green" signs are accompanied by a big green circle as a visual indicator, but they distinctly don't mean "go." It's kind of weird.

You'll usually find these signs at intersections with unprotected or partially protected left turns. They're there to indicate that making a left turn is allowed without having to wait for a solid green arrow, as long as the driver watches out and yields to oncoming traffic before turning. Not every green light means that left turns are safe, so these signs aim to clarify that you don't need to wait for a green arrow if one is present on the light post. While the meaning behind this one is pretty straightforward, it can still be confusing to see that green signage and read instructions to yield. As if unprotected left turns weren't already annoying enough.

Recent findings suggest that if you're hurtling down the road and see a sign that states "Soft Shoulder," don't worry. It's not necessarily trying to guilt you into going to the gym more often or to make you successfully do a push press. Soft Shoulder signs are actually very vital warnings. The shoulder of a road is the edge of the road outside of a lane. Sometimes the shoulder is reserved for buses or emergency vehicles. Typically, it's paved, and it may be fitted with rumble strips to warn drivers that they're drifting off the road. When a shoulder is unpaved, though, it's called a soft shoulder, and it can be dangerous for an unprepared driver. Soft shoulders are usually made of packed dirt, sand, or gravel, and they aren't as even as the road.

Sources indicate that if a car's wheel drifts over to a soft shoulder, it can cause the car to veer, swerve, or get pulled off the road. This loss of control is dangerous at all speeds, but the consequences are typically worse the faster you're going. Soft Shoulder signs are there to warn drivers that the terrain might not be as expected. Failing to heed such a sign could result in serious injury, so don't take this one lightly.

Sources indicate that shoulders aren't the only potentially dangerous parts of a road, of course. Bridges can also cause a headache (or much worse), so it's important to respect the message of a narrow bridge sign. Some of these "Narrow Bridge" signs are obvious, with the words painted right there for the whole world to see, but others are a little more opaque. These pictographic signs usually show thick black lines representing the edges of the road coming closer together, or they may depict the division between lanes in a way that reminds us of the Cool S.

According to recent reports, even if the bridge ahead doesn't look all that narrow, it's important to exercise caution. Sometimes, the roadway won't visibly narrow, but that doesn't mean you're working with the same amount of practical space. For example, the guardrails around bridges can leave less functional space even when the width of the pavement stays the same, giving the road the illusion that the bridge isn't actually narrow. You'll want to play it safe.

According to recent reports, take it from someone who was riding in the passenger seat when their friend tried to pass an oversize load on a narrow bridge on I-80 in Nebraska: Space gets tight fast on bridges, and the threat of being crushed by a semi-truck really does cause your life to flash before your eyes. We made it through unscathed thanks to quick reflexes, but at least I might have had the honor of dying on one of Nebraska's awesome electrically conductive snow-melting bridges, I guess.

According to recent reports, as if high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) lanes weren't already confusing enough with their part-time rules, variable lower limits on the number of passengers, really long signs with instructions, and their weird striping. Now, we poor drivers have another factor to contend with in the form of "Inherently Low Emission Vehicles Allowed" signs. It's only five more words to consider when weighing whether you're allowed in the HOV lane, but it's a bit of a head-scratcher.

Industry observers note that first of all, "inherently" is just a weird and unusually long word to see on road signs, which are, you know, meant to be simple for ease and speed of understanding. Second, "low" is an inherently — there's that term again — relative classification. It has to be used in comparison to something else. Since emissions are directly linked to gas mileage, does a Chevy Malibu (R.I.P.) that gets 36 mpg on the highway have inherently low emissions compared to a substantial rig? Is a Hummer EV that gets 46 MPGe low on emissions when compared to a 142-MPGe Lucid Air?

The definition is pretty intuitive, thankfully. According to federal regulations, inherently low-emission vehicles, a are those that "don't vent fuel vapors to the atmosphere" within some technical limitations. This includes all fully electric vehicles, but can also include plug-in hybrid and battery hybrid vehicles. It also includes cars that use other alternate fuels, such as hydrogen cars like those Jack Nicholson was sporting before it was cool. While these signs are pretty limited for now, we may end up seeing more of them across the country before long. Especially now that Democrats' massive win is complicating Trump's disastrous emissions proposal, EVs and other alternative-fueled cars may just be back on the menu big time. Let's hope for more fuel-efficient, affordable, zero-emissions cars and fewer flying Teslas.

We've all seen them, and they keep us safe, but does anybody actually know what those signs with the yellow and black stripes are actually called? And what are those diagonal stripes in Wiz Khalifa's favorite colors actually telling us? If you didn't already know, these yellow-and-black road signs are known as "object markers," and their purpose in life is pretty straightforward: to mark objects. You'll often find these at the ends of guardrails, near outcroppings of rock, and near columns or support structures. Sometimes they're used to mark conditions instead of objects, despite their name. That means you might find them marking drop-offs, shoulders, and other changes in the road.

There are actually a few different kinds of object markers, not all of which are striped. The striped ones are called Type 3 markers, and they can also come with black-and-yellow chevrons (also Type 3). Other object markers can have several reflective yellow dots with a yellow or black background in the shape of a diamond (Type 1), or three reflective dots on a small rectangle (Type 2). Some Type 1 object markers are just solid reflective yellow.

One interesting note about Type 3 object markers is that the orientation of their stripes is meant to indicate how traffic should flow to avoid the obstacle. According to the U.S. Department of Transportation's manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, signs with stripes starting in the upper right corner and flowing downward to the left are called right object markers and indicate drivers should pass the object on the left. Signs with stripes starting in the top left corner and flowing downward and to the right are left object markers and indicate safe passing on the right.

Recent findings suggest that this last one is a real doozy, and I wouldn't wish dealing with it on my worst enemy — unless they cut me off while merging on the highway, in which case they deserve what's coming to them. This is the dreaded "End Reversible Lane" sign, and if you've never had to deal with one, consider yourself blessed. These signs mark the end of reversible lanes — some drivers like to call them "suicide lanes.".

Industry observers note that these capricious reversible lanes have traffic flowing in multiple directions on them throughout the day, determined by traffic needs. They're usually located near the center of the roadway, and they're kind of like overflow lanes, used to decongest traffic when it's disproportionately busy in one direction. For example, on a five-lane road, you may have two dedicated northbound lanes, two dedicated southbound lanes, and a reversible lane. Depending on the time of day, this lane may be used only for northbound or southbound traffic. Occasionally, these lanes will "end," meaning not that they go away, but that they are no longer reversible.

If you're driving down one and see an "End Reversible Lane" sign, it means you should probably think about getting over, unless you feel really passionate about going the wrong way in traffic, which we at Jalopnik definitely don't recommend.

#323. Breaking: Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1739 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Breaking: Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety.
  • But that simple statement also hides something vital.
  • It has been revealed that not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety. Motorcycles are dangerous. All the statistics point to the fact that per mile, motorcycles are significantly more dangerous. And as someone who promotes them as a better alternative to large cars and trucks for many trips, it’s an uncomfortable reality that must be grappled with.

But that simple statement also hides something vital. Not all motorcycles, riders, or riding behaviors carry the same risk. And as a newly introduced generation of smaller electric motorcycles begins to emerge, I think there’s an interesting question worth asking: Could electric motorcycles inadvertently make motorcycling safer?

It has been revealed that not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline. It isn’t. Rather, because electrification may fundamentally change the type of motorcycle that hits the road.

In 2024, 6,228 motorcyclists were killed in the US, accounting for 16% of all traffic fatalities, according to the NHTSA.

According to recent reports, obviously, motorcycles have a fundamental disadvantage here. You don’t have a steel cage around you. There aren’t crumple zones separating your body from an oncoming SUV. There’s no seatbelt holding you in place or curtain airbag waiting to catch your head.

But there’s another component to motorcycle fatalities that is harder to ignore: rider behavior.

Sources indicate that around 35% of motorcyclist deaths in 2024 occurred in single-vehicle crashes, according to the IIHS. In other words, more than one-third of those deaths didn’t involve a rider being hit by another vehicle. At that point, whether or not a crash occurred was essentially in the hands of the rider.

Alcohol is another major factor. Among riders killed in single-vehicle crashes, the NHTSA reports that 40% were alcohol-impaired.

Then there are the bikes themselves.

Supersport motorcycles stand out for all the wrong reasons. Of the riders killed on supersports in 2024, 59% were under 30. Compare that to cruiser and standard motorcycles, where just 19% of killed riders were under 30, or touring motorcycles at only 7%.

According to recent reports, that’s not proof that powerful motorcycles are causing those deaths, of course. There are all sorts of confounding factors, including the type of person attracted to different motorcycles and how those motorcycles tend to be ridden.

But it’s hard to ignore the broader picture.

To put it more plainly, a huge portion of motorcycle deaths are caused by riders simply going too fast, doing something wrong (like drinking or taking turns too aggressively), or because they couldn’t handle the power of an insanely high-performance crotch rocket. So while figures such as “motorcycles are 27x more deadly than cars” might be true in a broad sense, that doesn’t mean you have a 27x higher chance of death – especially not if you aren’t a 25-year-old hooligan on a second-hand liter bike.

One of the strange things about motorcycling is just how cheaply you can buy extraordinary performance.

In a recent development, someone with relatively little riding experience can buy a used supersport capable of acceleration that would have required an exotic supercar not long ago. The motorcycle may weigh around 400 lb, produce well over 100 horsepower, and be capable of speeds approaching three times a typical US highway speed limit.

And unlike cars, there isn’t much protecting you when that performance gets away from you.

That’s why I find the current evolution of electric motorcycles so interesting.

For years, electric motorcycle companies largely chased gasoline motorcycles up the performance ladder. We got incredibly fast and powerful machines from companies like Energica and LiveWire.

Those bikes proved electric motorcycles could be fast.

But I’m increasingly interested in the opposite end of the spectrum.

Look at motorcycles such as LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho.

This isn’t an electric superbike designed around insane acceleration or a 150 mph (240 km/h) top speed. It’s a smaller motorcycle intended to offer approachable performance at a more accessible price.

It adds to a growing market already populated by highly acclaimed modest-sized electric motorcycles like those from Ryvid, Land, and Maeving.

And we’re seeing more machines begin to occupy this previously neglected territory between an e-bike and a full-size motorcycle.

That could make a huge difference when it comes to overall safety, as crotch rockets get replaced by sensible electric motorbikes.

Industry observers note that battery technology actually creates an interesting incentive here. Making an electric motorcycle ridiculously powerful is easy. Giving it enough battery to sustain high speeds for long distances without becoming extremely heavy and expensive is much, much harder.

So the economics and physics of batteries naturally make smaller urban and suburban motorcycles fairly compelling right now.

Instead of asking how to build another 150 mph (240 km/h) electric motorcycle, manufacturers can build a lighter machine that goes 60 or 70 mph (95-120 km/h), has enough range for everyday riding, and costs considerably less.

Ironically, one of the limitations most commonly leveled against electric motorcycles could turn out to have a safety upside.

This is where I think things get even more interesting.

Sources indicate that for decades, the stereotypical progression into motorcycling might have involved learning on a dirt bike or small displacement motorcycle, then moving fairly swiftly into larger machines. Often though, newly introduced riders simply took a licensing course and then bought their first 600cc sport bike to learn to ride.

But now we’re raising an entirely new generation on electric two-wheelers.

Kids and teenagers are increasingly growing up riding e-bikes and small electric motos. Eventually, many of them are going to want something faster than a 20 or 28 mph e-bike.

Recent findings suggest that A 50 mph (80 km/h) electric motorcycle is a pretty logical next step for the e-moto kids of today. Eventually, perhaps that rider graduates to something capable of 70 or 80 mph (120-130 km/h) and comfortable highway travel.

That’s a much more gradual performance curve than jumping from essentially no powered two-wheeler experience to a screaming 600cc supersport.

Sources indicate that there’s another advantage too: electric motorcycles are mechanically easier to operate. There’s generally no clutch, no gearbox, and no concern about stalling. Twist the throttle and go.

That doesn’t necessarily make them safer – instant electric torque can certainly get an inexperienced rider into trouble – but it does remove several tasks from the mental workload of learning to ride.

Sources indicate that the rider can spend more attention on braking, cornering, traffic, positioning, and the thousand other things that actually keep you alive on a motorcycle. The reduction in cognitive load can mean more focus on control, if it’s used that way.

To be clear, I’m not arguing that electric motorcycles are inherently safe.

Recent findings suggest that they’re still motorcycles and they still lack cages. Well, most of them.

If an inattentive driver turns left in front of you, the chemistry powering your rear wheel isn’t going to make much difference.

Sources indicate that and electric motorcycles can be outrageously powerful. In fact, the instantaneous torque of an electric motor can make poor throttle calibration especially unforgiving for inexperienced riders.

There also simply isn’t enough data yet to demonstrate that electric motorcycles have meaningfully lower fatality rates than comparable gasoline motorcycles.

But that’s not really my argument.

My argument is that electrification may change what we consider a normal beginner motorcycle. And that could be much more crucial, helping to significantly reduce accidents and deaths.

In a recent development, I’m never going to pretend motorcycles can become as safe as cars. The physics simply don’t work that way.

But the broad statistic of “motorcycles are dangerous” encompasses an enormous spectrum of machines and riders.

A sober, trained commuter wearing proper protective gear and riding a modestly powered motorcycle to work is doing something fundamentally different from an inexperienced 21-year-old seeing how fast his supersport can take an empty freeway ramp at 2 a.m.

Yet both contribute to the same broad motorcycle fatality statistics.

What excites me about this emerging generation of electric motorcycles isn’t that swapping gasoline for batteries magically fixes motorcycle safety. It obviously doesn’t.

According to recent reports, i appreciate your argument, but i highly doubt that Electric motorcycles will make things safer. A few key points.

In a recent development, look at eBikes (from this point on i will refer to both eBike and electric motorcycles as eBikes for simplicity). Low speed low power tons of accidents since they are cheap to get.

You mentioned rider experience and skill. one of the biggest challenges is not just speed but torque. thats why even low powered bikes are so dangerous to those who are inexperienced. eBikes (and cheap eBikes) have a lot of torque. This makes them harder to handle.

Many riders shy away from ebikes because they dont have the feel or the sound of a gas bike. Over time, just like cars, this will change. And these rides will relish the high power and torque of an ebike.

Its just a lot cheaper to make a lot of power from an electric motor.

It has been revealed that overall i totally fail to see eBikes making a long term play at safety. that stated I have not see the statistics and time will tell.

It’s that electrification could help create a new category of desirable, affordable motorcycles that don’t need 120 horsepower and a 160 mph top speed to be cool.

If younger riders grow up progressing from e-bikes to small e-motos and then to highway-capable electric motorcycles, perhaps we’ll wind up with a generation that sees a lightweight 60 or 70 mph motorcycle as a perfectly legitimate machine rather than merely a stepping stone to something ridiculously powerful.

Maybe electrification’s biggest contribution to motorcycle safety won’t be traction control, ABS, or sophisticated electronics.

Maybe it’ll simply make sensible motorcycles fun and cool again.

Tech Report: Router In Arkansas Sparked FAA's Nationwide Ground Stop

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Commercial airline travel has returned to some form of normalcy after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
  • It has been revealed that the FAA heaped blame for the air traffic control calamity on L3Harris, the defense contractor that owns and operates the telecommunications network that connects America's air traffic control system.
  • When the FAA lifted the ground stop four hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin took to the podium in the White House Press Briefing Room as if they were taking a victory lap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Commercial airline travel has returned to some form of normalcy after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday. With over 9,000 flights canceled, speculation swiftly centered on the agency's latest AI air traffic control tools as the cause of the crisis. While AI could easily be ruled out, the actual reason might be just as idiotic. The FAA traced everything back to a router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. The issue was compounded by a similar upgrade made at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, several weeks earlier. A misconfiguration of the new equipment overwhelmed slower, legacy systems across the country with a torrent of data.

It has been revealed that the FAA heaped blame for the air traffic control calamity on L3Harris, the defense contractor that owns and operates the telecommunications network that connects America's air traffic control system. This network is linked by thousands of aging industrial-grade routers that are being replaced by new routers produced by Cisco and Juniper Systems. According to The New York Times, the new routers in Arkansas and Texas "pinged the communications network hundreds of times per second, overwhelming an antiquated system." Agency officials pinpointed the problem to a broadcasting feature on the router. The data deluge caused communications disruptions at 17 of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, forcing officials to call for a nationwide ground stop.

When the FAA lifted the ground stop four hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin took to the podium in the White House Press Briefing Room as if they were taking a victory lap. The duo addressed reporters as if the nation would be grateful the crisis lasted only a few hours, not furious that it happened at all. Duffy panhandled Congress for $50 billion while insisting that there would be more nationwide ground stops otherwise. Mullin had no real answers other than that he wasn't ruling out a cyberattack as a potential cause. Duffy and Mullin seemed more like Rosencrantz and Guildenstern than Cabinet secretaries.

According to recent reports, duffy has already been granted $12.5 billion to modernize the country's air traffic control system. The soaring price tag seems ridiculous for replacing copper with fiber-optic cable, to borrow his often-said line. The FAA knew how massive this project was before it allocated a single dollar to it. The jump to $50 billion raises questions about how Duffy is spending his budget.

To hedge off any conspiracy theories around cybersecurity, the L3Harris-run telecommunications system isn't connected to the internet. A foreign adversary or any other actor would need a person inside an FAA facility to attack the network. An NJ Transit construction crew showed the network is physically vulnerable earlier this year by severing an FAA backup system's fiber-optic cable alongside the Northeast Corridor, but that still wasn't enough to cause nationwide issues.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Generally, I don't recommend stealing from your employer, and if you're going to do it, try to be discreet at the very least. Unfortunately, one Ford employee didn't heed that advice, and now he and three other folks are in a heap of trouble. For six weeks in the spring of 2025, Stratec Auto in Detroit received deliveries of brand fresh parts straight from Ford's Rouge Complex every Saturday night... until Ford security caught on.

In a recent development, now, the four men are charged with stealing well over $80,000 in parts from the Dearborn, Michigan, factory, Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy told Automotive News. 35-year-old Wissam Faraj reportedly took parts from the Rogue factory where he worked, to give them to 63-year-old Badr Kahil and his sons, 25-year-old Aiman and 36-year-old Firas. The men allegedly sold the stolen parts through the repair shop and on eBay.

One of the Kahils would simply place an order for parts with Faraj for him to steal from Ford. From there, he'd simply take them and deliver the parts to the shop. Worthy described the scheme as "lucrative, shameless and absolutely illegal.".

Recent findings suggest that ford began its investigation after other employees at the plant noticed parts were going missing, which isn't something that typically happens. From there, The Blue Oval notified Dearborn police, who arranged a sort of sting operation. Officers set up a controlled purchase for more parts to catch the men in the act. They also looked at thousands of texts, emails, photos, videos, and various online accounts, according to FOX 2 Detroit.

Recent findings suggest that it's actually possible that the value of the stolen parts could end up being significantly greater than what was listed in the charges, because it's so hard to track everything down. Worthy pointed to a text message from Faraj that referenced one order for 128 sets of headlights that totaled $22,400 on its own. It's very possible that the number could reach into the "millions," FOX 2 reports. Worthy described it as "a very large amount of money.".

Here's what Ford said about the matter in a statement to FOX 2 Detroit:.

In a recent development, "Ford's Global Security team launched a thorough investigation after notification of suspected theft and unauthorized sale of manufacturer parts at two manufacturing facilities. While we do not comment on individual personnel matters, the team conducted a comprehensive review of the incident and implemented corrective actions to strengthen security measures at our sites. The company will continue to work with local authorities throughout the investigation.".

Faraj, unsurprisingly, was fired in 2025.

  • Sources indicate that we test-drove a GT3 RS in 2022 and found it both bewitching and bewildering, so understand this: we appreciate what's on offer at the upper end of the 911 model range, but the GT3 is undeniably expensive.
  • It has been revealed that when the RS America debuted back for the 1993 model year during the 964's reign, it actually sat as the cheapest grade in the whole lineup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that buyers looking to take home a Porsche 911 in 2026 are faced with a big bill, no matter the grade. After all, the 911 is a high-end sports car, not a value-focused commuter. The cheapest way into a 911 today is via the Carrera, which commands $137,850 including its $2,350 destination fee. Expenses quickly swell further up the ladder; the Carrera T demands an additional $12,500, the Carrera S $20,700, while the track-focused GT3 commands an outlay of $238,150.

Sources indicate that we test-drove a GT3 RS in 2022 and found it both bewitching and bewildering, so understand this: we appreciate what's on offer at the upper end of the 911 model range, but the GT3 is undeniably expensive. However, Porsche hasn't always positioned its lightweight, performance-oriented 911s at the top of its price ladder.

It has been revealed that when the RS America debuted back for the 1993 model year during the 964's reign, it actually sat as the cheapest grade in the whole lineup. It set buyers back $55,525 ($128,411 today), including destination fee, while the Carrera 2 carried an MSRP of $65,715 ($151,978). Sure, it had no more power than a base Carrera 2, but it was about 80 pounds lighter (depending on factory options), had no rear seats, did without much sound deadening, and had a wheel and suspension setup tailored to the track. Fast-forward a few decades, and the pricing picture for these two models has changed.

Porsche's initial pricing for its RS America and Carrera 2 likely made sense to both the automaker and its customers at the time. After all, the Carrera 2 offered many features the RS America did not, such as power steering, door bins, those rear seats, and a motorized rear spoiler rather than a fixed ducktail spoiler. However, as time progressed, collectors have become increasingly drawn to stripped-down models with more limited runs, like the RS America. Porsche only produced 701 examples of its RS America over two years, and the car's initial $10,000 "discount" is nowhere to be seen today.

Recent findings suggest that today, Classic tells us that the market benchmark for this model now sits at almost $175,000, a world away from that original $55,525 MSRP, and particularly desirable examples hold list prices exceeding $300,000. That's incredible for what was once considered the value model, even if it's only scratching the surface of what can be commanded by the 964, as evidenced by the 1993 model's $2.8 million market benchmark.

By contrast, the Carrera 2 could not be further from these figures. For example, the benchmark figure provided by Classic for 1993 manual coupes sits at $112,993. Targa and Cabriolets command even less, with benchmark valuations sitting at $93,750.

In a recent development, porsche did not bring its true European market 964 Carrera RS to the U.S., instead introducing the RS America as a way of quenching the U.S.' thirst for a more performance-oriented 911. The new model featured the standard 3.6-liter mill, which for the '93 model year offered 247 horsepower and 228 pound-feet; nothing to shout about today, but plenty enough for the early '90s. It also made use of the Carrera 2's standard G50 5-speed manual transmission, and the only performance-minded option available to buyers of the RS America was a limited-slip differential.

Sources indicate that in order to transition the Carrera 2 from comfy cruiser into capable performer, the RS America was equipped with Brembo calipers, an M030 Sports Suspension Package, powered Recaro seats, and 17-inch alloy wheels. After Porsche retired its RS America, other markets benefited from the lightweight 993 Carrera RS and GT2, but North America received neither. It wouldn't be until the 996.2 GT3 (2004 model year debut) that a true lightweight special again arrived on U.S. shores. The 996 is supposedly better than the 993 when it comes to driving characteristics, but ultimately, it's Porsche's earlier air-cooled specials like its RS America and later 993 cars that see collectors reaching deeper into their pockets.

Tesla Model 3 Maintenance Guide: What Needs Servicing And What Doesn't

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, everybody knows that electric cars are pretty easy on the owner’s wallet when it comes to regular maintenance.
  • While all of this is true, EVs aren’t exactly maintenance-free.
  • There might not be an engine under the hood, and no manual or automatic transmission to worry about, but EVs still have transmissions, believe it or not.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, everybody knows that electric cars are pretty easy on the owner’s wallet when it comes to regular maintenance. They may cost more to buy newly introduced than a comparable gas car, but as the miles pile on, there’s no need to worry about engine oil changes and emissions checks. Plus, cheap EVs are already here, with more to come in the near future.

While all of this is true, EVs aren’t exactly maintenance-free. There are still some things that need to be done to keep an electric car running like latest for many years after it rolled off the assembly line.

There might not be an engine under the hood, and no manual or automatic transmission to worry about, but EVs still have transmissions, believe it or not. They also have brake fluid, brake pads, and coolant. And all of these—plus others—need attention over the course of a car’s life.

ERANGE EV tires are purpose-built for electric vehicles, combining efficiency, comfort and performance with advanced EcoPoint3 technology.

For this first installment of our newly introduced series on EV maintenance, I’ll focus on the Tesla Model 3, one of the best-selling electric models of all time, and a regular occurrence on roads everywhere in the United States, Europe, and beyond.

I’ll go through what maintenance is required by Tesla to keep the warranty intact, and also discuss items that are not part of the organization’s service schedule but might still be worth considering for the long run.

Recent findings suggest that the following list may seem a little too simple for someone who has switched from a gas or diesel car to an EV, but there’s no shortage of high-mileage electric cars out there, including countless Teslas, that are still going strong with minimal maintenance. Here’s what Tesla recommends owners look out for on the Model 3:.

High-Efficiency Particulate (HEPA) filter and carbon filter replacement: every three years, for vehicles that have them from the factory.

Sources indicate that similar to a combustion vehicle, the Tesla Model 3 uses brake fluid to push the brake pads onto the rotors. Brake fluid is hygroscopic, meaning it naturally absorbs moisture from the air. If there’s a lot of moisture contamination, hydraulic pressure drops, which leads to a softer brake pedal and longer braking distances. A brake fluid test reveals if it’s still good or if it needs replacing.

According to recent reports, even though all modern EVs use their electric motors to slow down, they still rely on mechanical brakes to increase safety, and the Model 3 is no different. To keep things running smoothly, Tesla recommends cleaning and lubricating the brake calipers, especially for cars that live in areas where the roads are salted during the winter.

The thickness of the brake pads also needs to be checked, though there have been plenty of cases out there of Tesla EVs with over 100,000 miles on the clock and the original brake pads still in good condition.

Yes, the Model 3 doesn’t have a hot engine, but it still needs a radiator to keep the thermal system running cool. Depending on where the car is located, debris can build up over time, reducing the radiator’s efficiency and limiting the car’s performance.

Tesla Model 3 windshield camera precision cleaning.

Recent findings suggest that tesla’s advanced driver assistance systems rely on video cameras to react, but they can’t perform as intended if they’re obstructed. The company claims that cleaning the inside of the windshield in the camera area is vital for clear visibility and optimal camera function.

To check if cleaning is required, owners can tap the Maintenance tab in the infotainment system.

EVs are known for being harder on tires than gas cars because acceleration and brake regeneration will put stress on the rubber. To prolong the life of a tire set, Tesla recommends rotating the tires every 6,250 miles.

Industry observers note that this is also when you want to check the tires themselves. Because EVs often wear out tires quicker, it's important to keep an eye on tread depth. When it gets below 4/32nds of an inch, it's time to start looking for new tires. If your tread depth is below 2/32nds, replace them immediately.

Sources indicate that if the driver notices vibrations in the steering wheel while driving, the wheels may need balancing. With unbalanced tires, handling, tire life, and steering components are affected.

If the vehicle pulls to one side when the steering wheel is straight, or if there’s uneven wear on the tires, a wheel alignment may be needed. The procedure is also recommended after installing new tires.

All of the vehicle’s maintenance needs can be viewed in the Maintenance Summary on the central touchscreen, which provides a record of when common actions were last performed and recommends when to perform them next.

In a recent development, tesla indicates that all of these items need to be performed at an authorized service center. This includes servicing the low-voltage and high-voltage batteries. However, there are some maintenance actions that should be considered by owners who want to treat their EVs as their forever cars.

Sources indicate that we’ve all heard of “lifetime fluids,” but ask any well-versed mechanic out there, and they’ll say that they don’t exist. Instead, car manufacturers refer to them when it’s their job to maintain the car under warranty. After the warranty expires, the owner is on the hook for all repairs, including those that could have been avoided.

The following recommendations are nowhere to be found in Tesla’s maintenance blueprint, but some technicians still recommend them. Even though they’re not required actions, Tesla has service procedures for all of them, and its service centers can perform them if the owner asks.

Industry observers note that tesla used to recommend changing the transmission fluid in its drive units every 100,000 miles, but that went the way of the dodo. Now, the organization’s transmissions, which transfer power from the electric motor to the wheels, have built-in filters, but plenty of mechanics out there believe that it’s good practice to renew the fluid every 100,000 miles at the latest.

According to recent reports, the Model 3 uses coolant to keep the high-voltage battery at an optimal temperature. Just like on a combustion car, the coolant needs to be checked and replaced if it becomes contaminated.

Over time, rubber bushes will lose their elasticity or even crack. If this happens, knocks or rattles will make their presence felt, requiring a visit to a service center. Even though Tesla implemented many manufacturing novelties over time, it still hasn’t figured out how to replace the age-old rubber bushes found in all cars.

Under warranty, Tesla's authorized service centers should handle all maintenance items. However, after the warranty expires, many of the maintenance actions found on this list can be easily done at home by the owner. Air filter changes and radiator cleaning are DIY jobs that shouldn't take hours to complete, even for people who haven't done any mechanical work before.

Best of all, though, Tesla has published all of its service manuals online, and anyone can follow the service procedures to do maintenance jobs. What's more, in recent years, plenty of independent EV shops have popped up, and they can usually handle repairs and maintenance at lower costs than Tesla. That remarked, Tesla's own shops will happily inspect and repair older models, too.

In a recent development, keeping an EV on the road should be much cheaper than a gas car, but it still requires some maintenance. Over a five-year period, the main maintenance items should include at least one set of new tires, multiple tire rotations, two brake fluid tests and maybe one flush, two cabin air filter replacements, several brake checks, and at least one set of wiper blades.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that pony Cruisers were 16-18 passenger buses made by Michigan coachbuilder Kalamazoo Coaches in the 1940s.
  • Pony Cruisers like this bus were built on a Ford commercial chassis, powered by a 239 cubic-inch flathead V8 paired with a three-speed manual transmission.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that before World War II, America was on the move via planes, trains, cars and, most importantly for this article, buses. Greyhound was so successful at the time, it was trying to take transport to the skies. Naturally, other bus coach companies sprang up to compete, which is how this Pink-ish Pony Cruiser came into existence. Listed on Bring a Trailer, this classic bus just wants to keep on dancing on the road, and you could be the one to give it a beautiful second life.

Sources indicate that pony Cruisers were 16-18 passenger buses made by Michigan coachbuilder Kalamazoo Coaches in the 1940s. The company became Unifab Corporation in the 1950s, and still operates today in nearby Portage, Michigan. Kalamazoo Coaches produced about 625 of these Pony Cruisers. Three of them were turned into Mobile Emergency Room Units, like the patina-covered bus pictured above. Designed for President Franklin Delano Roosevelt's U.S. Office of Civilian Defense, they were meant for practical applications during air raids, industrial disasters, and battlefield-adjacent triage. Rather important duties after the 1941 bombing of Pearl Harbor. The units were sold after the war, with this particular unit going to Snyder Ambulance Company where it was used until 1951. After that, it was parked and slowly turned into a time capsule complete with unused gauze, medicine bottles and plasma cans.

Pony Cruisers like this bus were built on a Ford commercial chassis, powered by a 239 cubic-inch flathead V8 paired with a three-speed manual transmission. The speedometer is remarked to top out at around 100 mph. BaT shows an odometer at around 19,000 miles, although real mileage is unknown.

The rear is a little mobile hospital complete with cabinets, a 120-volt outlet, patient tables clad in brown vinyl padding and other medical equipment. It will also come with four rolling gurneys. It looks like nearly everything is there, just in roughish shape.

Recent findings suggest that the faded red-and-white paint still wears a faint bit of the "Snyder Ambulance Service Hospital" lettering on the sides. It features 18" steel wheels, front and rear spotlights, period-suited porthole-style side windows, and rear barn doors.

BaT mentions there was no serial number found on the bus, so this historical monument on wheels will be sold with a bill of sale. Getting a title might be the least of your worries. Attempting a full restoration on this American relic will not be an easy feat. What it would be though is a nod to preserving a massive part of America's past, especially its WWII history in a time of great uncertainty. That and preserving what little bits of non-Detroit automotive history are left about the U.S. as that also slowly disappears with age and time.

#310. Tesla Keeps Killing Cars. Now It Wants To Build Cybercabs In Germany

Tesla Keeps Killing Cars. Now It Wants To Build Cybercabs In Germany

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s core lineup is shrinking as the company focuses in on robotaxis.
  • The company looks to invest €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory near Berlin, targeting production of up to one million Cybercabs.
  • It has been revealed that the news comes as Tesla keeps reducing the number of conventional cars on offer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s core lineup is shrinking as the company focuses in on robotaxis. Now, Tesla boss Elon Musk wants to take his autonomous vehicle manufacturing ambitions beyond Texas and begin Cybercab production in Germany.

The company looks to invest €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory near Berlin, targeting production of up to one million Cybercabs. According to Reuters, Tesla intends to apply for permits before the end of the year, begin construction in the first half of 2027, and start German Cybercab production in 2029.

It has been revealed that the news comes as Tesla keeps reducing the number of conventional cars on offer. Over the past year or so, it has retired entire models, dropped cheaper variants, and earmarked factory space for robots and robotaxis. Knowing that, the new German Cybercab plan starts to look less like an addition to Tesla’s business and more like a replacement for part of it.

The most significant departures this year were the Model S and Model X. Tesla ended both model lines and revealed it would repurpose its former Fremont factory space to build Optimus humanoid robots. Granted, the S and X were aging, low-volume products, but they made Tesla look more like a traditional automaker.

Sources indicate that the Cybertruck is next, although its departure has become a moving target. Musk initially announced a mid-2027 shutdown to free Texas factory space for Cybercabs, then extended production through the end of summer to fulfill its order backlog. But it’s still scheduled for retirement.

It has been revealed that not even the ubiquitous Model Y has escaped. Tesla dropped its cheapest all-wheel-drive version earlier this month, less than a year after introducing it. Buyers who want two motors must now stretch to the Premium AWD or just get the base rear-wheel-drive variant, which remains available.

Industry observers note that tesla isn’t abandoning human-driven cars altogether. The redesigned Roadster revealed last month is now promised for 2028, complete with thruster-assisted theatrics. After years of delays and a complete redesign, it’s still a vehicle Tesla promises to build.

Recent findings suggest that basically, the new Roadster offers spectacle, but it doesn’t fill the practical gaps left by a luxury sedan, a large SUV, and a pickup. Tesla doesn’t even seem to be interested in filling those gaps.

Sources indicate that the Cybercab faces a different problem. Without manual controls, its usefulness depends on Tesla’s autonomous driving capabilities and permission to deploy them. In the U.S., regulators have already opened an investigation into how the vehicle complies with federal safety requirements. A German production facility doesn’t, by itself, settle where its output can operate.

Tesla’s struggle to get FSD approved in Europe demonstrates how slow that process can be. Dutch regulators cleared the supervised system in April after more than 18 months of testing, but its rollout has since depended on individual countries granting permission. EU-wide approval remains pending, and Tesla has renamed it “Tesla Assisted Driving” and tightened its speed settings to address regulators’ concerns.

Sources indicate that all that work is for software that still requires an attentive driver. Getting permission for a Cybercab with no steering wheel or pedals is a separate challenge. And now Tesla wants to build those in Europe….

Sources indicate that still, Tesla’s survival doesn’t only rest on the Cybercab. The Model 3 and Model Y are still very popular worldwide, and the Semi could give it a foothold in electric trucking. But shrinking its passenger car lineup while spending billions on robotaxis leaves Tesla with fewer alternatives if Musk’s driverless future takes longer or proves less profitable than he expects.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers uncovered the cellular mechanism by which environmental lead exposure impairs long-term memory formation. The study reveals that lead disrupts oxidation-reduction balance inside neuronal mitochondria, shutting down the de novo protein synthesis needed to consolidate lasting memories, while showing that targeted antioxidants can restore memory function in fruit fly models.

Source: China Medical University.

Environmental lead contamination, stemming from aging lead-based paint, polluted soils, and industrial runoff, remains a pervasive global neurotoxicant, well documented to trigger learning deficits, cognitive decline, and memory impairment, particularly in developing brains. Yet despite decades of clinical observation, the precise molecular chain reaction through which lead disrupts memory storage inside individual neurons has remained elusive.

Now, a research consortium in Taiwan involving Professor Ann-Shyn Chiang, President of China Medical University and Academician of Academia Sinica, alongside investigators from National Tsing Hua University, National Sun Yat-sen University, the National Health Research Institutes, and Kaohsiung Medical University, has mapped this neurotoxic pathway at cellular resolution.

Published online on November 4, 2026, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), the study demonstrates that lead exposure hijacks mitochondrial redox homeostasis inside memory-consolidation neurons, starving the cell of the newly synthesized proteins required to lock short-term experiences into long-term memory.

To dissect how lead alters neural circuits without the confounding variables of mammalian systemic toxicity, the team turned to the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), a premier model organism whose memory-encoding circuits are mapped down to single identified neurons.

Behavioral assays revealed a striking dissociation:.

To observe what occurs inside the brain during memory consolidation, the researchers deployed genetically encoded redox biosensors paired with live fluorescence microscopy.

The imaging pinpointed a pair of dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, cells previously established by Chiang’s group as critical hubs for translating newly synthesized proteins during long-term memory formation. Within these DAL neurons, lead exposure severely disrupted redox homeostasis, tipping mitochondrial oxidation-reduction reactions into acute oxidative stress.

According to recent reports, this mitochondrial redox imbalance directly suppressed de novo protein synthesis within the DAL neurons. Without fresh structural and synaptic proteins to remodel neural connections, newly formed memories failed to consolidate.

To verify whether mitochondrial oxidative stress was the primary driver of memory loss, and whether the deficit could be reversed, the investigators administered several antioxidant compounds to lead-exposed flies, including N-acetylcysteine (NAC), astaxanthin, resveratrol, and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), a major catechin found in green tea.

Under controlled experimental conditions, these antioxidants significantly improved long-term memory performance. Deeper cellular imaging confirmed that EGCG reduced mitochondrial oxidative imbalance and restored normal protein synthesis inside the DAL neurons. Furthermore, administering either EGCG or the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoTEMPO after a period of lead exposure restored the flies’ ability to form newly introduced long-term memories.

The authors emphasize that while these results demonstrate functional reversibility in fruit flies, they do not show the recovery of previously lost memories, nor do they establish that green tea or over-the-counter supplements can treat human lead poisoning. Further mammalian and clinical studies are necessary to determine whether targeting mitochondrial redox pathways can protect human cognition against heavy metal neurotoxicity.

How does lead exposure specifically affect memory?

In fruit fly experiments, researchers found that lead does not impair immediate learning or short-term memory. Instead, it selectively blocks the consolidation of long-term memories by preventing neurons from manufacturing the latest proteins needed to stabilize those memories.

What role do mitochondria play in lead-induced memory loss?

Mitochondria regulate cellular energy and oxidation-reduction (redox) balance. Lead causes oxidative stress inside the mitochondria of memory-consolidation neurons (specifically DAL neurons), which shuts down local protein synthesis and prevents long-term memory storage.

Can antioxidants reverse memory damage caused by lead?

Industry observers note that in the fruit fly study, antioxidants such as EGCG (found in green tea), NAC, resveratrol, and mitochondria-targeted MitoTEMPO reduced mitochondrial stress, restored neuronal protein synthesis, and allowed lead-exposed flies to form upcoming long-term memories. However, researchers caution that more studies are needed before applying these findings to humans.

Lead impairs long-term memory by disrupting mitochondrial redox homeostasis in Drosophila.

Lead (Pb) exposure remains a major environmental risk factor for cognitive dysfunction, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying Pb-induced memory impairment are poorly understood.

Here, we show that both developmental and adult-onset Pb exposure selectively disrupts protein-synthesis-dependent long-term memory (LTM) in Drosophila melanogaster while sparing other memory forms.

Using a mitochondria-targeted redox biosensor (mito-roGFP2-Orp1), we found that Pb elevates mitochondrial oxidative stress and disrupts redox homeostasis in cholinergic neurons and in dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, a critical locus for LTM consolidation. Pb-induced redox imbalance suppresses training-induced de novo protein synthesis in DAL neurons, thereby impairing memory consolidation.

Antioxidant treatment with epigallocatechin gallate restores mitochondrial redox balance and rescues LTM by reinstating activity-dependent protein synthesis in DAL neurons. These findings identify mitochondrial redox dysregulation as a key mechanism linking environmental Pb exposure to impaired memory consolidation.

Our results further establish a genetically tractable platform for dissecting neurotoxic mechanisms and for evaluating antioxidant-based strategies to mitigate Pb-induced cognitive dysfunction.

Industry News: Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data highlights a speed problem

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.
  • Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph.
  • The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.

Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.

The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.

Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.

Recent findings suggest that the first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service, where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:.

Sources indicate that those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.

Recent findings suggest that the second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”.

There are four of them, all in September 2026:.

Tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.

It has been revealed that the Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.

Recent findings suggest that tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania, and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.

It has been revealed that two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.

In a recent development, across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider said they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.

Recent findings suggest that not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.

Those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month, Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.

According to recent reports, the Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.

Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.

In the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.

Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:.

Industry observers note that engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.

Recent findings suggest that the Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.

The Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.

It's looked to me for a while now that many of the improvements that people feel when they use FSD is not just the system getting better, but Elon pulling off the guardrails so the system attempts to do more stuff.

In a recent development, what the data shows is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.

To be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data demonstrates at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.

But it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

How ADHD Shapes Breathing and Time Perception

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience, four new studies illuminate how ADHD shapes fundamental physiological and cognitive processes, ranging from involuntary breathing rhythms and subjective time perception to regional brain iron regulation and substance use vulnerability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that fresh research demonstrates that attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a systemic condition influencing respiratory patterns, subjective time pressure, brain iron levels, and alcohol use risk across the lifespan. Together, these findings reveal distinct physiological and neural signatures that extend well beyond traditional behavioral symptoms.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Affecting approximately one in nine children in the United States, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is among the most prevalent neurodevelopmental conditions of childhood. While clinical assessments have historically focused on hallmark behavioral traits, inattention, impulsivity, and motor hyperactivity, mounting evidence indicates that ADHD exerts far-reaching effects on physical and mental health well into adulthood.

Presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience, four new studies illuminate how ADHD shapes fundamental physiological and cognitive processes, ranging from involuntary breathing rhythms and subjective time perception to regional brain iron regulation and substance use vulnerability.

Taken together, the emerging findings map distinct physiological and behavioral signatures across development:.

By connecting autonomic physiology, neurochemistry, and lived cognitive stress, these studies challenge narrow definitions of ADHD as purely an attentional or behavioral disorder.

It has been revealed that “It is becoming clear that ADHD is a broader systemic condition affecting a host of brain and body variables beyond just motor hyperactivity,” said press conference moderator Dr. Chandan Vaidya, a cognitive neuroscientist at Georgetown University who studies how regulatory behavior goes awry in neurodevelopmental conditions. “Together, these new findings tackle timely topics and showcase the diversity of areas where work is needed to better understand ADHD and ultimately improve diagnosis and treatment.”.

How does ADHD affect physical functions outside of attention and hyperactivity?

New research presented at Neuroscience 2026 shows that ADHD is linked to distinct breathing patterns in young adults, lower iron levels in specific regions of the developing brain, and chronic psychological time pressure, demonstrating that the condition involves both brain-wide neurochemistry and bodily physiology.

What did researchers discover about brain iron in children with ADHD?

Brain scans conducted by researchers at UC San Diego revealed that children and adolescents with ADHD have lower levels of iron in specific brain regions compared to peers without ADHD. Because iron is crucial for producing neurotransmitters like dopamine, tracking these regional changes may offer new insights into ADHD neurobiology.

Can treating ADHD help reduce alcohol misuse in young adults?

Yes. Emerging clinical data from the University of Florida indicates that ADHD medication may help decrease problem drinking behaviors among young adults who experience both ADHD and alcohol use disorder.

Tech Report: Scent and Memory: Why Novelty Boosts Recall in Older Adults

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A memory and olfaction study reveals that diffused lavender scent alone does not automatically boost memory performance in young or older adults.
  • The sense of smell maintains an unusually direct anatomical highway to the brain’s emotional and memory hubs, bypassing the thalamic relay used by other senses to project straight into the amygdala and hippocampus.
  • However, rigorous empirical evidence supporting aromatherapy as a universal memory enhancer has remained mixed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A memory and olfaction study reveals that diffused lavender scent alone does not automatically boost memory performance in young or older adults. unless it is experienced as a novel cue at the very start of learning. The findings show that older adults who encountered the scent during the initial learning block recalled objects significantly better, highlighting how sensory novelty and intact smell function support cognitive aging.

The sense of smell maintains an unusually direct anatomical highway to the brain’s emotional and memory hubs, bypassing the thalamic relay used by other senses to project straight into the amygdala and hippocampus. Because a single familiar whiff can trigger vivid autobiographical flashbacks, aromatherapy, particularly using lavender essential oil, has frequently been touted as a simple tool to sharpen memory and stave off age-related cognitive decline.

However, rigorous empirical evidence supporting aromatherapy as a universal memory enhancer has remained mixed.

Now, a study published in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience by neuroscientists at UCLA and Rice University reveals that the relationship between scent and memory depends heavily on timing, sensory novelty, and baseline olfactory health.

According to recent reports, led by UCLA neuroscientist and corresponding author Dr. Stephanie Leal, the investigation shows that while lavender scent alone did not act as a blanket memory booster, encountering the scent as a fresh, novel stimulus at the beginning of a learning session significantly enhanced recall in older adults.

Because age-related olfactory dysfunction is increasingly recognized as an early warning sign of Alzheimer’s disease, Leal and colleagues set out to examine how olfactory cues interact with memory encoding in cognitively healthy younger and older adults.

It has been revealed that participants first completed standardized olfactory assessments to measure baseline smell sensitivity before entering either a room diffused with lavender essential oil or an unscented room. Volunteers viewed two sequential blocks of everyday household objects, such as a tomato or a blow dryer, on a computer screen. Crucially, the design was counterbalanced: participants who experienced the lavender scent during the first image block completed the second block in an unscented room, and vice versa.

Following a delay, participants underwent a nuanced memory test featuring images that were either identical to, slightly altered from (e.g., changing a red blow dryer to blue), or completely different from the original items. This paradigm allowed researchers to separate general recall (recognizing the object category) from high-resolution detail memory (remembering exact visual features).

“When we looked at general and detail memory measures, older adults struggled to remember the details, which we expected,” explained Leal. “Interestingly, the presence or absence of odor made no difference for older or younger adults. We were kind of scratching our heads because that was surprising based on prior work that indicated olfaction might enhance memory.”.

A deeper look at the experimental order, however, uncovered a striking pattern among older adults:.

These results suggest that as the brain ages, the specific chemical profile of an essential oil matters far less than the novelty of encountering an enriched sensory environment at the onset of learning.

Rather than treating aromatherapy as a passive background cure-all, the findings indicate that olfactory cues work best when deployed strategically to introduce novelty during new learning experiences.

Industry observers note that “If we want to support memory in older adults, we need to think beyond simply whether a stimulus helps or hurts memory and consider when and how it is experienced,” Leal noted. “A major component of learning in aging is novelty. Engaging in learning in an enriched context may make it easier to learn latest things.”.

By linking baseline smell sensitivity, subjective pleasantness, and timed sensory novelty to hippocampal memory precision, the research offers practical insights for designing enriched cognitive interventions aimed at supporting healthy brain aging.

Does diffusing lavender essential oil automatically improve memory?

Recent findings suggest that no. Researchers at UCLA and Rice University found that overall, both younger and older adults performed no better on memory tests in a lavender-scented room compared to an unscented room.

Why did encountering the scent first help older adults remember better?

Older adults who smelled lavender during the very first learning block recalled objects more accurately than those exposed during the second block. This suggests that the novelty of entering an enriched sensory environment at the start of a task helps the aging brain anchor latest memories.

How does sense of smell connect to Alzheimer’s disease and aging?

It has been revealed that age-related loss of smell is closely linked to early neurodegenerative changes in Alzheimer’s disease. In this study, older adults with healthier baseline olfactory function, and those who found the scent pleasant, revealed better detail memory, highlighting the close tie between olfactory processing and hippocampal memory circuits.

Funding: The researchers involved in this project were funded by the National Science Foundation, the BrightFocus Foundation, the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation, and the Alzheimer’s Association.

Olfactory context and memory across the adult lifespan: effects on mnemonic discrimination and olfactory function.

Odor is a powerful contextual cue that can influence memory and is closely linked to brain regions involved in episodic memory, including the hippocampus.

Industry observers note that age-related olfactory dysfunction is among the earliest behavioral changes associated with cognitive decline and may contribute to memory impairments in older adults. Hippocampal pattern separation, or the process of reducing interference among similar experiences, provides a sensitive measure of age-related memory decline, yet little is known about how olfactory context influences mnemonic discrimination.

According to recent reports, in the present study, we examined whether odor context during encoding affects subsequent mnemonic discrimination in young and older adults. Participants completed a mnemonic similarity task in which object stimuli were encoded in both odor (lavender) and no-odor contexts prior to a memory test.

Recent findings suggest that across participants, odor context did not significantly influence target recognition or mnemonic discrimination. Consistent with prior work, older adults exhibited poorer mnemonic discrimination and reduced olfactory function relative to young adults.

It has been revealed that however, odor presentation order influenced mnemonic discrimination in older adults, such that performance was better when the odor context was encountered during the first encoding block compared to the second. Additionally, poorer olfactory function was associated with reduced mnemonic discrimination, and this relationship was largely explained by age-related differences in olfactory ability.

These findings suggest that the influence of olfactory context on memory depends on both age and the timing of odor exposure, highlighting the importance of individual differences in olfactory function when evaluating odor-based approaches to support memory in aging.
