📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that have you been looking for some new reading material, something amusing, maybe strange, or even alarming? Have you thought about perusing automotive service bulletins? Probably not. But we're a bunch of incurable car nerds here at Jalopnik, so service announcements are exactly the kind of thing we might read over our morning bowl of Cheerios.

It turns out there's some entertaining — and sometimes surprisingly concerning — stuff in those bulletins. For example, did you know that a little nest of spiders could cause $300 worth of damage in some Chevy vehicles? That's not all. Some General Motors (GM) vehicles repeatedly prank-called OnStar for a while, and it turns out that the rugged full-size 2024 and 2025 Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra were no match for car washes. You might also be surprised to learn that safety features like airbags and automatic emergency brakes can turn on you, and that a leaky roof can cause your key fob to stop working — and then there are all of the strange noises and odors.

In a recent development, you might expect some newly introduced cars to have problems or bugs that need to be corrected under warranty — maybe a transmission that doesn't shift right, some early coolant leaks, or a leaky sunroof. One thing you don't expect from a new car is it making prank calls to OnStar. Yet, according to one GM service update for the 2007 GMC Sierra, certain 2001-2008 light-duty trucks, Hummers, and even Saabs were exhibiting a "condition to which the vehicle owner/operator would be unaware of resulting in repeated incomplete calls to the OnStar being made." So, maybe instead of prank calling, it's more accurate to say the vehicles were doing the automotive electronic equivalent of butt dialing. The solution was a recall where the dealer would replace the OnStar Module (VCIM).

Sources indicate that GM had acknowledged similar problems in an earlier service bulletin for the 2006 GMC Canyon, applicable to 1996 through 2008 OnStar-equipped vehicles, but the company mostly blamed the problem on customers. One explanation involved the customer hitting the white button, followed by the system misinterpreting a random sound, or background noise such as a "cough," as an emergency. Really, a cough? What would it do in case of a loud sneeze? Deploy the airbags?

Listen, people, you've got to take care of your trucks. That means not doing recklessly negligent things like washing them. At one point, drivers of some 2024 and 2025 Sierra/Silverado 2500 HDs and 3500 HDs found their check engine lights were coming on. Dealership technicians would see that the trucks were kicking out a DTC P244B diagnostic code, or "Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too High Bank 1." The culprit? According to Bulletin No. PIP6020A (PDF), "Engineering has found that this code may set if the vehicle was recently washed.".

It has been revealed that but that's not the only way water has vexed GM vehicle owners. Some owners of 2021 Chevy Tahoes and GMC Yukons were hearing "gurgling noises" after heavy rains and, you guessed it, car washes. It turned out to be residual water in sunroof drain tubes. The fix was to turn on the HVAC blower in fresh air mode to blow out the remaining water.

At first, the Cybertruck was the only truck that would get messed up by car washes, as the simple act of taking a Cybertruck through a car wash could brick it and possibly void its warranty. GM followed suit, though the worst its trucks could muster was a measly check engine light.

Modern cars come with lots of safety features to help you avoid accidents. Unfortunately, those safety features can sometimes go rogue. The Cadillac XT4 comes equipped with automatic emergency braking, which will stop the car if it detects an obstacle before the driver sees it. We imagine it's probably prevented more than one distracted driver from rear-ending a stopped car. That's all well and good until the car starts coming to a halt for objects that aren't there. That's exactly what some 2024 XT4s were doing, as reported by Service Bulletin 24-NA-053 (PDF). Yikes.

According to recent reports, we'd hate to have that happen to us when we're trying to merge onto the freeway while everyone else is going 80 mph. The bulletin remarked the cause "may" be limitations in the camera. The confidence conveyed there is very reassuring. Of course, that's not as scary as the time GM recalled several cars due to temporary loss of braking.

In a similar case, Program Bulletin 12084 (PDF) alerted dealers that the Sensing and Diagnostic Module on some 2013 Chevy Malibus could reset itself after a hard braking event, a process that lasted three seconds. If the driver were to execute an "aggressive" turning maneuver during those three seconds, the side airbags could deploy. Or, if there was an accident during those three seconds, the seatbelt pretensioner might not work. These scenarios seem oddly specific, causing us to think that maybe this actually happened more than once.

Everyone knows that one friend who is, shall we say, "hygiene-challenged" and would benefit from a good shower. Perhaps among carmakers, GM is that friend, considering how many service bulletins have to do with odd smells emanating from their vehicles. These odors range from annoying to downright alarming.

For example, one GM Bulletin addressed gear oil smell in vehicles with remote vents. On the dangerous side, one safety recall of the Buick Regal GS and Pontiac Grand Prix said that owners may notice a burning smell, indicating a fire under the hood. Drivers of several 2022-2024 GM models noticed a smoke smell coming from under their seats, and technicians were likely to find "melted burn marks around the height adjuster motor.".

Meanwhile, one GM bulletin treated unwanted odors as a sales opportunity for its proprietary product, GM Vehicle Care Odor Eliminator. It pitched it to the dealerships to be used by their service center techs for detailing as well as prepping their used cars for sale. To be fair, some smells can make a car hard to sell. It suggested that the product be given as a gift with a fresh car sale, as in, "Here's a little something for those unpleasant odors that will inevitably plague your new car." According to GM, displaying it prominently for sale would "increase dealership traffic" since the product isn't sold in stores. Sure, we can see people beating down the door to get their bottle of GM Vehicle Care Odor Eliminator.

Who doesn't like to hear a low growl that comes out of a powerful internal combustion engine? It's disturbing, though, to hear a growl when you put the car in park, whether the engine is running or not, but drivers of certain 1980 Oldsmobile Ninety Eights were hearing a growl when they would park the car on an incline. The GM bulletin that addressed this directed that drivers be told to engage the parking brake before shifting into park, then make sure the car is really in park.

It has been revealed that what is the opposite of a growl? Chirps and squeaks might make good candidates. Those are the noises that have been coming out of some 2019-2023 model full-size trucks and SUVs. If we buy a full-size pickup with a huge V8, chirps and squeaks are not the kind of noises we want to hear coming from the engine. According to Bulletin 26-NA-021, ticks, taps, and typewriter noises have been heard coming from 2019 – 2026 Trucks. That has to be disconcerting.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Bulletin 14-06-04-004G remarked that GM vehicles equipped with a two-stage vane-type oil pump have been known to make "Rrrrp" or "Rasp" noises when the engine starts in freezing weather or if the engine has been sitting for a few hours. Even weirder, the same bulletin said that vehicles equipped with a 6.2-liter engine may let out a "moan" after a cold start, at idle, or during operation at low RPMs. What's really weird is that GM says that all of these noises are normal.

Recent findings suggest that key fobs stop working from time to time. When it happens to us, we order a new battery from Amazon and call it a day. However, it has never occurred to us to check the car's roof. GM Service Bulletin 23-NA-107 (PDF) addressed pinhole leaks that would sometimes occur in the 2024 Chevy Trax. Oddly enough, that could cause the key fob to stop working. Apparently, water would get into some of the electronics, which somehow impacted the connection with the key fob. We have to give kudos to the engineer or technician who put two and two together and figured this out.

Key fobs don't have to be malfunctioning to help with troubleshooting, though. Some owners of the 2023 Cadillac XT4 and 2024 and 2025 Buick Envision had complained that the lights would flash when the vehicle was parked and the battery would be drained until it died. GM remarked this was likely caused by a defect in the K171 Rear Closure Hands Free Module. How could the tech tell for sure that this was the cause? Easy. The bulletin said to tape the key fob to the rear wiper. If the rear gate opens when the lights flash, it must be the K171 Rear Closure Hands Free Module. Again, we marvel at the mind that was able to connect the dots in this way.

No one likes to see the check engine light come on, but it was showing up on the dashboards of certain Buick Encore, Chevy Trax, and Chevy Sonic models during the 2010s for a surprising reason. Those vehicles were kicking out P0446 or P0455 error codes, indicating a restriction in the EVAP canister. Inconvenient, sure, but not strange — except that the service bulletin instructed technicians to check the EVAP canister for spider nests. We don't know why spiders liked this part so much or how many times techs found spiders in these EVAP canisters before this bulletin was put out, but apparently it happened enough for GM to rule arachnids as the likely cause.

You'd think that the remedy would just be to evict the spiders from the EVAP canister. Nope. GM said that the entire EVAP canister would need to be replaced. That's a $300 part. Who knew that a nest of spiders could do so much damage?

In a recent development, you might not think it, but service bulletins can make for an entertaining read, and we've just skimmed the surface with the examples we've covered here. If you're bored, you can check out more GM bulletins on the tech giant's official website, and let us know in the comments if you come across any gems you find interesting.

#300. Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system.
  • Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.
  • Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to fresh analysis from energy think tank Ember.

Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.

Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.

The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup.

It has been revealed that solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls.

That matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that in the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12.

The savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%.

“We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” remarked Daan Walter, principal at Ember.

Recent findings suggest that by combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy.

The researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years.

It has been revealed that that’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average.

Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output.

The findings also raise questions for developers planning new fossil fuel plants.

Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%.

In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper.

Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW.

For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics.

Ember’s interactive Wind + Solar + Battery Atlas lets consumers explore reliable electricity costs in their own region.

Only lessees of the 2026/2027 Mercedes CLA, 2027 GLC Electric SUV2, S-Class Sedan, GLE SUV and Coupe, and GLS will be eligible.

Following is a statement from Ani Dasgupta, President and CEO, World Resources Institute:.

Recent findings suggest that “One message came across loud and clear from world leaders: climate action has shifted from an environmental movement to a core economic and security imperative. Sources indicate that “Electrification and the transition away from fossil fuels rightly took center stage. These are two vital, intertwined goals, and progress on one must reinforce the other. “President Lula deserves credit for keeping the transition away from fossil fuels at the top of the international agenda and delivering a global roadmap that countries can adapt to their own circumstances. Australia and Türkiye now have an opportunity to lead by example, putting forward their own transition looks and encouraging others to follow.

Industry observers note that “Vulnerable countries delivered an equally clear message: access to affordable finance is critical to them implementing their climate ambition. High borrowing costs and unsustainable debt are holding back investment in the very countries that need it most. With the $1.3 trillion finance goal established, the focus is shifting to how all sources of finance can work together to deliver investment at scale and how we ensure affordable capital reaches those who need it most. There are encouraging signs, including an influx of pledges from philanthropies for the Brazil-initiated Tropical Forests Forever Facility.

It has been revealed that “Adaptation and early warning systems received much-needed attention after a year of crushing heatwaves, fires, and floods. But that attention now needs to turn to the investment in systemic resilience as the best way to make economies and societies stronger and improve people’s lives. Building more resilient cities was a major focus and will take deep collaboration between national governments, cities, and states. Cities are on the front lines of delivering the climate solutions and essential services that make people’s lives better, and demonstrating these benefits is critical to accelerating the transition. Cities and local communities especially need greater access to adaptation finance.

It has been revealed that “It was disappointing to see no dedicated ocean event at the Leaders’ Summit, despite over 90% of countries including ocean action in national climate looks. Ocean-based solutions can provide up to one-third of the emissions cuts needed by 2050 to keep 1.5°C within reach. This ambition for ocean action must be reflected in any COP31 cover decision and translate into concrete progress, especially for vulnerable coastal and island nations.

International cooperation on climate may be changing shape, but it is still alive and needed now more than ever. #297. Industry News: Older Brains Lose Synchronization Between Movement and Body Temperature

Industry News: Older Brains Lose Synchronization Between Movement and Body Temperature

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A chronobiology study in mice reveals that while the brain’s 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, shorter multi-hour “ultradian” rhythms in physical activity and core body temperature significantly weaken.
  • Throughout every 24-hour day, mammalian physiology follows an intricate temporal choreography.
  • Layered atop this overarching 24-hour cycle are faster, multi-hour biological oscillations known as ultradian rhythms, which pulse every few hours to coordinate bursts of activity, metabolic demand, and thermoregulation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A chronobiology study in mice reveals that while the brain’s 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, shorter multi-hour “ultradian” rhythms in physical activity and core body temperature significantly weaken. Simultaneously, aging decouples movement from internal temperature regulation and triggers neuroinflammatory gene shifts, glial remodeling, and neuronal loss inside the brain’s master circadian clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).

Throughout every 24-hour day, mammalian physiology follows an intricate temporal choreography. Governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a tiny cluster of neurons in the hypothalamus that acts as the brain’s master biological clock, core body temperature, hormone release, and physical activity rise and fall in predictable ~24-hour circadian rhythms.

Layered atop this overarching 24-hour cycle are faster, multi-hour biological oscillations known as ultradian rhythms, which pulse every few hours to coordinate bursts of activity, metabolic demand, and thermoregulation.

While age-related sleep fragmentation and impaired temperature regulation are well-documented clinical hallmarks of aging, precisely how ultradian rhythms evolve across the lifespan, and how they relate to cellular changes inside the SCN, has remained poorly understood.

Now, a comprehensive chronobiology investigation examining mice across the adult lifespan (from 3 to 21 months of age) reveals that while the 24-hour circadian framework remains detectable in old age, the faster 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms deteriorate, accompanied by a breakdown in coordination between physical activity and internal body temperature.

To separate externally driven daily routines from internally generated biological timing, the researchers continuously recorded locomotor activity and core body temperature in mice across multiple age brackets under both standard 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycles and constant darkness, an experimental condition that removes environmental light cues to expose the brain’s intrinsic pacemaker.

The physiological telemetry revealed a striking divergence between macro- and micro-rhythms:.

To explore the neural underpinnings of these physiological shifts, the investigators analyzed cellular architecture and gene expression profiles directly inside the SCN of young and aged mice.

Even though core circadian clock genes continued cycling, the cellular microenvironment of the aging SCN showed pronounced signs of biological wear:.

By demonstrating that shorter ultradian rhythms and temperature-activity coupling falter even when overall 24-hour circadian rhythmicity persists, the findings offer a fresh lens through which to view age-related sleep disturbances and vulnerability to heat or cold stress.

Further experimental work will determine whether targeting neuroinflammation or supporting glial-neuronal communication inside the SCN can restore ultradian stability, potentially paving the way for interventions that alleviate sleep fragmentation and thermoregulatory decline in older adults.

What is the difference between circadian rhythms and ultradian rhythms?

In a recent development, circadian rhythms are biological cycles that repeat roughly every 24 hours, such as the daily sleep-wake cycle. Ultradian rhythms are shorter biological cycles that repeat multiple times within a single day, typically every 2 to 6 hours, regulating smaller bursts of physical activity, alertness, and core body temperature fluctuations.

How does aging affect these biological rhythms?

Industry observers note that researchers found that while older mice kept their basic 24-hour rhythms and core clock gene cycles, their shorter 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms weakened significantly. Furthermore, physical movement and internal body temperature became disconnected, no longer rising and falling together as closely as in younger animals.

What changes happen inside the brain’s master clock during aging?

Inside the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the brain’s master clock, aging was linked to increased activity of immune-related genes, changes in supportive glial cells, and a reduction in neuron density, which may impair how the brain coordinates fine-tuned daily bodily rhythms.

Funding: This study was supported by JSPS KAKENHI (grant numbers JP21K19287, JP21H05036, JP23H04941, and JP22K21351); AMED (grant number JP21zf0127005); JST CREST (grant number JPMJCR24T4); JST SPRING (grant number JPMJSP2124) and the World Premier International Research Center Initiative (WPI).

Aging remodels the suprachiasmatic nucleus and weakens ultradian rhythms and activity–temperature coupling.

Aging alters daily physiology, but how these changes relate to remodeling of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) remains incompletely understood.

Here, we examined time-resolved SCN transcriptomic profiles alongside longitudinal recordings of core body temperature and locomotor activity, using separate cohorts for the molecular and physiological analyses.

Aging was associated with extensive SCN transcriptomic remodeling, including enrichment of innate immune, interferon-related, complement-associated, and glial programs, while selected canonical clock genes retained detectable rhythmic expression.

In a recent development, the composition and temporal profiles of broader rhythmic transcriptional programs also differed between young and aged SCN samples. Aged mice retained detectable circadian rhythms but demonstrated reduced 2–6 h ultradian wavelet power in locomotor activity and body temperature, lower activity–temperature correlations, and altered optimal integration windows and time-of-day-dependent relationships. Histological analyses revealed glial remodeling and reduced neuronal marker-positive cell density in the aged SCN.

These findings identify parallel age-associated changes in SCN molecular and cellular organization and in physiological rhythmic power and activity–temperature associations.

JLR's all-electric baby Defender is coming soon. According to Car and Driver, JLR boss PB Balaji recently noted on an earnings call that the smaller, all-electric Defender will go into production at the end next year, alongside the upcoming Range Rover GT. There's no official name for the bite-sized Defender, but Balaji reportedly didn't want to call it the Defender Sport.

There's not much word on any technical specs just yet, but EMA supports 800-volt architectures and is capable of housing both pure battery-electric powertrains and hybrids. The baby Defender could very well offer both, but whichever powertrain it has, it'll need to be capable off-road to deliver on its name.

According to Motor1, Mark Cameron, managing director of Defender and Discovery brands, said "We have got to make sure everything we do as Defender has the DNA of the brand: epic built-to-last, go-anywhere capability.".

Pricing, specs, and range are all still under wraps, although it might make sense for either fresh electric product to have the same 118.5-kWh battery as the current Range Rover Electric. With it, the electric Rover is capable of 333 miles of range, and that uses a conventional platform. The battery is also capable of 350 kW DC fast-charging, which would be very competitive in the segment, so it might make sense for JLR to roll with that battery tech. The major Range Rover Electric has a dual-motor powertrain, with 542 horsepower, but that might be a bit much for a baby Defender. Although, there could be a go-fast version with that much power, similar to the current Defender Octa.

According to recent reports, land Rover pushed the current full-size Defender's electric replacement out to sometime in the 2030s, so there shouldn't be any confusion between the full-size and bite-size models. If production begins in late 2027, that means we could see the baby Defender soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers discovered that taste buds actively process and filter mixed flavors before sending signals to the brain. The study indicates that sour stimuli trigger serotonin release inside taste buds, dampening neural responses to sweet, bitter, and salty flavors while downstream neurons sort tastes into two broad categories: pleasant or unpleasant.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Biting into a tart lemon bar or sipping a sweet-and-sour beverage delivers a complex blend of chemical stimuli to the tongue simultaneously. For decades, neuroscientists have worked to determine whether the brain mixes these individual flavor signals centrally, or whether taste buds themselves edit and shape flavor combinations before a single electrical impulse ever leaves the tongue.

It has been revealed that in a study published in Journal of Neuroscience, neuroscientists led by Dr. Stephen Roper at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine recorded gustatory nerve signaling in mice exposed to mixed taste solutions.

The findings reveal that sourness exerts a dominant, suppressive effect over other primary tastes right inside the taste bud, driven by local serotonin signaling.

To trace how mixed tastes travel from peripheral receptors to the central nervous system, Roper and colleagues measured neural responses along the gustatory pathway while exposing mice to single tastes and multi-taste mixtures.

Comparing neural firing across taste conditions revealed two striking principles of gustatory coding:.

To uncover how sourness mutes competing tastes so early in the sensory pipeline, the investigators zeroed in on serotonin, a neurotransmitter released inside each taste bud by specialized sour-responsive receptor cells (Type III taste cells).

Manipulating local serotonin levels directly controlled the strength of flavor suppression:.

These results demonstrate that taste buds function as miniature computational hubs, using paracrine serotonin signaling to inhibit neighboring receptor cells before gustatory information is handed off to cranial nerves.

It has been revealed that “Taste buds not only respond to and transduce taste compounds, they also integrate and manipulate gustatory signals before transmitting them to the brain,” explained Roper. “The neurons that collect signals produced in taste buds are themselves organized into two large groups or clusters, neurons that convey gustatory signals associated with pleasure and neurons that convey unpleasant taste signals.”.

By establishing how peripheral serotonin signaling shapes flavor dominance and how downstream neurons sort palatability, the study lays groundwork for identifying the genetic signatures of pleasure- versus aversion-coding taste neurons, and exploring whether targeted molecular interventions could one day modulate taste perception in clinical nutrition or sensory disorders.

Why do sour flavors overpower sweet, salty, and bitter tastes?

Researchers at the University of Miami found that sour-responsive cells inside taste buds release the neurotransmitter serotonin. This local serotonin dampens the signals of neighboring sweet, bitter, and salty receptor cells before the taste information even reaches the nerves leading to the brain.

Do taste buds simply send raw flavor data to the brain?

Industry observers note that no. The study shows that taste buds act like miniature processing centers that actively mix, filter, and modify taste signals locally before transmitting them to sensory neurons.

How do taste nerves organize flavors on their way to the brain?

According to the researchers, the sensory neurons collecting signals from taste buds are broadly organized into two major functional groups: neurons that carry pleasant taste signals and neurons that carry unpleasant taste signals.

Sour Suppresses Sweet, Salty, and Bitter: Implications for Signal Processing in Taste Buds.

Taste is typically encountered as complex blends, yet how peripheral taste organs process heterogeneous mixtures remains poorly understood. Here we asked how sour stimuli influence the encoding of sweet, salty, and bitter tastes in primary gustatory sensory neurons.

Using in vivo calcium imaging in mice of either sex to record neurons in geniculate ganglia during oral delivery of tastants, we compared responses to naturally occurring taste stimuli presented alone versus in binary mixtures that activate acid (sour)-sensing (Type III) taste bud cells. Adding citric acid or HCl robustly suppressed sucrose-evoked responses in geniculate ganglion neurons, even though acid itself did not activate those neurons.

Acid-induced suppression generalized to bitter and salty tastes, which, like sucrose, are believed to activate Type II taste cells. Additional stimuli that activate acid-sensing taste cells (NH4Cl, KCl) also reduced sucrose responses, supporting a common mechanism linked to Type III cells. Manipulating levels of serotonin (a paracrine transmitter released by Type III cells) in taste buds altered taste suppression: increasing serotonin with 5-hydroxytryptophan enhanced acid-induced suppression whereas depleting serotonin with para-chlorophenylalanine weakened it.

It has been revealed that finally, population analyses, including UMAP dimensionality reduction, indicate that taste suppression is not limited to a particular subset of gustatory sensory neurons. The findings are consistent with serotonin-dependent paracrine inhibition within taste buds as a contributor to sour-driven suppression in taste mixtures and reveal a compression of gustatory information into hedonic categories as early as at the level of primary sensory neurons.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cummins is withdrawing from upcoming electrolyser sales, but its customers have a problem that cannot be handled by closing a sales office. In September, its Hydrogenics subsidiaries recommended that customers stop using HyLYZER electrolysers following a review of operating data. The company disclosed the recommendation in its November quarterly report, said that it had not released a recall, and was still assessing what modifications might be needed for equipment to return to service. It had not established the cost of resolving the matter and warned that the eventual financial effect could be material.

Cummins had a substantial position in the PEM electrolyser business. Accelera reports more than 45 HyLYZER 500 systems and more than 20 HyLYZER 1000 systems rated at 5 MW each. Using those minimum reported system counts and equipment ratings, its historical deployments represent roughly 145–213 MW, equivalent to 11–16% of the IEA’s projected 1.3 GW global PEM installed base at the end of 2026. Cummins has not published the number of HyLYZER plants covered by its September recommendation. The company is leaving a sizeable equipment estate requiring expert maintenance, field engineers and potential safety modifications.

Recent findings suggest that the timing makes the situation consequential. Cummins announced in February that it intended to cease new commercial electrolyser activity, while continuing existing customer commitments. Its 2025 Accelera restructuring and impairment charges reached $458 million across several actions, including the electrolyser retreat. It is reducing specialist capacity at the same time as installed equipment needs engineering attention. Revenue from new orders can disappear faster than warranties, service obligations and safety responsibilities.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing on Cummins’ hydrogen hangover examines the HyLYZER warning, the customer projects and the financial implications of manufacturers leaving shrinking markets. The underlying evidence and project comparisons are in the full analysis.

The problem now moves from selling hardware to keeping it safe and serviceable. Investigating field data, testing modifications, certifying repair procedures and maintaining proprietary controls requires specialist teams. Those teams must remain capable long after the sales pipeline and the business unit built around it have contracted.

Industry observers note that estonia’s Stargate Hydrogen has taken over Cummins’ legacy HySTAT alkaline electrolyser platform and supplies replacement stacks and service for a fleet of more than 400 installations. That handover shows how intellectual property, manufacturing capability and field-service expertise can survive an OEM exit. Cummins’ HyLYZER PEM fleet needs its own engineering and aftermarket solution.

Sources indicate that for owners, the financial question also depends on the purpose of the hydrogen. Air Liquide’s 20 MW Bécancour installation and Linde’s 35 MW Niagara Falls project serve companies with industrial hydrogen customers and alternative supply networks. Interruptions can mean lost sales, replacement purchases and costs of maintaining customer commitments. An owner with contracted industrial demand has a commercial reason to restore production, provided the equipment can meet the required safety standards and the replacement supply costs justify it.

Florida Power & Light’s Cavendish project presents another decision. Its 25 MW HyLYZER installation converts electricity to hydrogen for limited blending into natural gas used in power generation. Even without a stop-use concern, that application has to compete with using electricity directly or obtaining reliable grid services by other means. At an illustrative 55 kWh/kg of electrolyser electricity and 60% combined-cycle generation efficiency, about 36% of the original electricity returns after converting it to hydrogen and burning it, before compression and storage. Input power at $50/MWh would cost roughly $138/MWh of recovered electricity before equipment and operating expenses. Repairing the electrolyser would not change that conversion arithmetic.

It has been revealed that the economic difference appears again at Hysolar’s Nieuwegein installation. A 2025 KWR H-Flex evaluation documented project delays, higher costs and hydrogen demand expanding more slowly than planned. Its electrolyser, dedicated pipeline, refuelling station and vehicle customers are linked by a common demand forecast. Better equipment performance helps only when enough customers will buy the hydrogen at prices covering production and delivery. The same distinction applies to demonstration projects combining buses, heating, electricity and gas blending: several proposed uses do not guarantee several profitable markets.

In a recent development, manufacturers face the cost of retaining the people and intellectual property to support complex equipment long after the expected growth market has contracted. Cummins’ separate exit from its low-pressure fuel-cell business illustrates the potential bill: in March 2026, it made a $175 million net payment as part of a sale, cancellation of commitments and claims settlement, producing a $199 million accounting charge. Those are fuel-cell transaction figures, not estimated HyLYZER repair costs. The PEM matter remains unquantified.

The customers’ cost can exceed the repair bill. Owners need a safe restart route, long-term supply of stacks and controls, a price for replacement hydrogen during outages, and buyers able to pay for the output afterward. Lenders face a thinner resale market for specialised plants when their OEM leaves. Public funders face grant, regulated cost-recovery and guarantee liabilities when projects stop operating.

The wider hydrogen market makes these questions urgent. The IEA’s Global Hydrogen Review 2026 finds that global demand still sits overwhelmingly in traditional industry and refining. Only about one-fifth of newly signed low-emissions hydrogen offtake volumes in 2025 had firm contractual commitments. A producer, refuelling-station operator and vehicle buyer can each invest on the assumption that the other two will grow. That is one demand risk distributed across three balance sheets, not three independent investments.

According to recent reports, the next investment decision needs a safe route back to service, contracted customers, dependable parts supply and a costed exit alternative. Governments should direct support toward industrial customers who need hydrogen and can pay for it, rather than finance energy-carrier applications that lose to direct electricity. Cummins is exposing the long tail of earlier commitments. Other suppliers, buyers and lenders still control their next decisions.

Sources indicate that the complete Cummins analysis compares industrial-gas plants, fuel-substitution pilots, refuelling systems and legacy equipment obligations. The earlier Cummins–Alstom assessment highlights how similar service liabilities can persist in fuel-cell transportation.

A massive neuroimaging investigation involving 2,187 patients with multiple sclerosis reveals that grey matter atrophy does not accumulate at random; rather, it radiates outward from specific cortical and subcortical “disease epicenters.” Published by Mar Barrantes-Cepas and colleagues, the study provides strong clinical evidence for the “nodal stress hypothesis.”.

The authors demonstrate that high-degree topological network hubs, such as the visual, sensorimotor, and temporal cortices, alongside the thalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala, are selectively vulnerable to neurodegenerative collapse because their intense metabolic demands exhaust local cells. The findings also document transneuronal degeneration propagating along structural connections, confirming that progressive neurodegeneration in multiple sclerosis occurs independently of acute inflammatory relapses.

According to recent reports, multiple sclerosis (MS) has long been defined as a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammatory demyelinating lesions scattered across the white matter of the central nervous system. Yet in recent decades, advanced neuroimaging has revealed an equally devastating, covert pathological hallmark: widespread, accelerated grey matter atrophy.

Unlike transient focal inflammation, grey matter volume loss begins during the earliest clinical stages, correlates directly with irreversible physical disability and cognitive decline, and progresses relentlessly even when disease-modifying therapies effectively suppress clinical relapses.

For years, the spatial patterning of this tissue loss remained elusive, presenting in non-random yet seemingly disparate cortical and subcortical distributions.

Now, in an extensive multicenter neuroimaging study evaluating MRI scans from 2,187 individuals diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, a research team led by Mar Barrantes-Cepas and colleagues reveals the organizational logic behind this neurodegenerative spread.

Their work substantiates the nodal stress hypothesis, demonstrating that grey matter loss originates within high-traffic, hyper-connected “disease epicenters” and propagates throughout the connectome via transneuronal degeneration.

To map the spatiotemporal evolution of brain atrophy, the researchers utilized structural MRI datasets from an international cohort of 2,187 patients across various stages and clinical subtypes of multiple sclerosis, comparing localized tissue loss against normative connectome architecture.

In a recent development, the analysis revealed that the earliest and most severe tissue loss localized within the brain’s primary topological hubs. These “epicenters” included:.

It has been revealed that these findings provide large-scale empirical backing for the nodal stress hypothesis. In complex network topology, hubs represent the most critical communication centers, routing traffic across disparate functional modules.

It has been revealed that however, this central positioning carries a severe bioenergetic cost. High-degree hubs maintain higher baseline firing rates, express higher densities of energy-intensive ion channels, and require disproportionate mitochondrial ATP production to preserve synaptic transmission.

Sources indicate that in multiple sclerosis, where chronic subclinical microglial inflammation, widespread demyelination, and oxidative stress compromise mitochondrial respiratory chain efficiency, these high-demand hubs become metabolic bottlenecks. The relentless functional demand exhausts cellular energy supplies, triggering localized axonal degeneration and neuronal apoptosis.

Recent findings suggest that the study demonstrated that once a disease epicenter begins to decay, the pathology does not remain confined. Instead, the scans revealed clear markers of transneuronal degeneration, a cascading process where damage in a primary hub travels anterogradely or retrogradely across anatomical white matter tracts to damage downstream connected neurons.

As high-traffic epicenters fail, their connected secondary and tertiary structural partners lose vital neurotrophic support and experience excitotoxic or disuse stress, causing neurodegeneration to systematically ripple through the structural connectome.

Crucially, the investigators tracked how these network-based degradation pathways differed across relapsing-remitting and progressive forms of the disease, finding that network-level strain drives disability accumulation across all cohorts.

“It is now clear that disease progression can occur independently of relapses and acute inflammation,” write Barrantes-Cepas and colleagues. “Network-based measures, which are easily obtainable from conventional MRI and normative datasets, could be used to explain future atrophy progression in individual patients.”.

The recognition that multiple sclerosis progression is driven by network-mediated metabolic exhaustion challenges the classical clinical focus on managing only acute, gadolinium-enhancing white matter lesions.

In a recent development, because conventional MRI scans routinely collected in routine clinical practice can be evaluated using normative connectome templates, network-based nodal stress modeling offers a low-cost, non-invasive prognostic tool. Clinicians could potentially map an individual’s specific epicenter vulnerability early in the disease course, forecasting spatial trajectories of grey matter loss years before clinical deficits emerge.

Furthermore, these findings highlight fresh avenues for neuroprotective drug discovery: therapies designed to bolster mitochondrial bioenergetics, protect against metabolic exhaustion, or buffer high-traffic hubs from metabolic overload could provide the missing therapeutic weapon needed to halt progressive disability in multiple sclerosis.

How does grey matter atrophy spread through the brain in multiple sclerosis?

Recent findings suggest that atrophy does not spread at random. It originates in specific “disease epicenters”, the brain’s most heavily connected topological hubs, such as the thalamus, hippocampus, visual, and sensorimotor cortices. From these epicenters, damage propagates to distant brain regions along structural nerve pathways through transneuronal degeneration.

What is the “nodal stress hypothesis”?

Recent findings suggest that the nodal stress hypothesis suggests that brain hubs with the highest number of connections are under constant, intense metabolic strain because they must process and route massive amounts of neural communication. In multiple sclerosis, where energy production is already impaired, these high-traffic hubs suffer metabolic exhaustion, making them the first to degenerate.

Can multiple sclerosis worsen without relapses or acute inflammation?

Sources indicate that yes. This study confirms that progressive neurodegeneration and brain volume loss can proceed independently of acute clinical relapses and active autoimmune lesions, driven instead by chronic network-based metabolic failure and structural disconnectivity.

The role of network connectivity and transcriptomic vulnerability in shaping gray matter atrophy in multiple sclerosis.

It has been revealed that clinical progression is strongly linked to gray matter atrophy in multiple sclerosis (MS), detectable early on MRI and progressing nonrandomly across the brain. However, the mechanisms driving its spatiotemporal progression and individual variability remain unclear.

Sources indicate that using MRIs from 2187 participants, alongside normative data, we systematically investigated network-based mechanisms underlying MS-related atrophy. Regional atrophy was associated with functional cortical hubness, supporting the nodal stress hypothesis, and was constrained by anatomical and functional connections, consistent with transneuronal degeneration. Lesional disconnection and transcriptomic vulnerability played marginal roles.

Patient- and subgroup-level analyses revealed that network-based mechanisms are specifically linked to MS-related neurodegeneration and may operate differently in distinct subtypes or disease phases. Atrophy patterns were anchored to the connectivity profiles of disease epicenters involving the visual, sensorimotor, and temporal cortices, as well as the hippocampi, amygdalae, and thalami.

Network-based measures enhanced the explanation of future atrophy progression in people with MS, providing a mechanistic framework to understand neurodegeneration in MS.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that now, we'll get into some of the details about the Sprint ER below, but first let's head off some possible objections at the pass.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welp, we may have finally reached a turning point. Yes, short-sighted automakers have been supporting Trump's move to roll back fuel-economy standards. But voters seemed to have had other ideas on Election Day 2026, when the Dems secured both the Senate and House. Of course, while that may stop some of the madness, we're unlikely to see another fuel-sipper like the 1986 Chevrolet Sprint ER anytime soon. Chevy's tiny captive import originally posted an EPA highway rating of 60 mpg, a mark that no other non-electrified production car in the country has matched since. Plus, that highway score was complemented by ratings of 55 mpg in the city and 57 mpg combined.

It has been revealed that now, we'll get into some of the details about the Sprint ER below, but first let's head off some possible objections at the pass. The most notable is that the EPA made a major change in how it calculates fuel efficiency back in 2007 and then retroactively updated its database. As a result, the 1986 Sprint ER currently demonstrates an EPA line of 44 mpg city/53 mpg highway/48 mpg combined. That makes for decreases of approximately 20%/12%/16% compared to its original fuel-economy grades.

Some drivers have also topped 60 mpg in real-world diesel driving. A writer for Car and Driver, for example, hypermiled a 2017 Chevy Cruze diesel to the tune of 70 mpg over a test run of about 160 miles. It's just that diesel engines have some drawbacks of their own.

According to recent reports, in a way, the genesis of the Chevy Sprint goes back to some of America's earlier meddling in the Middle East. The CIA had put Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi in control of Iran in 1953 — forcing out that country's democratically elected prime minister — and the shah was then overthrown himself as part of the 1979 Iranian Revolution. That led to the oil crisis of the same year, which helped convince GM to enter a three-way partnership with Isuzu and Suzuki in 1981. The goal was to build high-efficiency cars that were, basically, too small for GM to build at the time.

One of those cars was the JDM Suzuki Cultus, a car that would be renamed the Swift in Europe in 1985 and be rebadged as the Chevrolet Sprint for the same year. It also served as the Pontiac Firefly, but only in Canada. Now, this wasn't as tiny as a kei car, but it certainly wasn't big. That 1986 Sprint checked in at 144 inches long, 60 inches wide, and 53 inches tall — so it was about 1 inch longer than the 2022 Chevy Spark, but also 2.8 inches narrower, 5.4 inches shorter in height, and 774 pounds lighter. After all, the Sprint ER, a three-door hatchback, tipped the scales at only 1,504 pounds.

Industry observers note that yet svelte dimensions weren't the only factors in play. The regular Sprint was motivated by a 1.0-liter I3 engine capable of 48 horsepower, and Suzuki had revised the camshaft for the ER version. It made a significant difference, since the non-ER model had an original EPA line of 44/50/47 (37/45/40 in today's ratings).

For this section, please keep in mind we're going to level the playing field by using the post-2008 EPA ratings for the Sprint ER — which, as a reminder, features a fuel-economy line of 44/53/48 with its standard five-speed manual gearbox. Nowadays, the most fuel-efficient non-electrified car in the country is the 2026 Honda Civic that can see 32/41/36 with its 2.0-liter I4 motor and CVT. The 2026 Civic Hybrid, as an FYI, can raise the efficiency bar to 50/47/49.

The latter model isn't the country's most efficient hybrid, either. For that, we have to turn to the Toyota Prius. Sure, it gets an electric boost from its hybrid setup, yet the Prius may be the next gas-powered car to reach the 60 mpg club. The latest EPA line, for the 2027 Prius, is 59/50/55. Oddly, the 2026 Prius is listed at 57/56/57, and Toyota hasn't revealed what's changed. The same year Prius further led the way among hybrids with the best real-world gas mileage, at least according to Consumer Reports.

And the most efficient EVs can routinely see triple-digit MPGe figures with the EPA. The Lucid Air Pure, with rear-wheel drive and 19-inch wheels, sets the pace in this regard. It can squeeze out 149 MPGe in the city, complemented by grades of 142 MPGe highway and 146 MPGe combined.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A psychological and sleep research study published in PLOS Mental Health reveals that people who frequently startle awake while drifting off to sleep, a phenomenon known as “sleep starts” or hypnic jerks, report significantly poorer sleep quality, greater insomnia severity, and heightened anxiety.

Conducted by Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus at Paris Lodron University Salzburg, the investigation examined 194 adults across Austria and Germany. The researchers discovered that frequent sleep starts do not merely represent isolated motor twitches, but manifest alongside autonomic surges, sensory flashes, and cognitive-emotional hyperarousal driven by unhelpful beliefs and acute pressure to fall asleep.

It has been revealed that just as consciousness begins to dissolve and the body relaxes into slumber, an abrupt, violent jolt shatters the transition. Often accompanied by the vivid sensation of tumbling into an abyss, an electric zap down the spine, or a blinding flash of light, the heart races as the sleeper gasps awake in sudden panic.

In a recent development, known medically as “sleep starts” or hypnic jerks, these sudden myoclonic twitches occur at the boundary between wakefulness and non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. While sporadic sleep starts are a benign, universal human experience, for a substantial subset of the population they recur persistently, transforming the threshold of sleep into a source of dread.

In a study published in the open-access journal PLOS Mental Health, researchers Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus of the Centre for Cognitive Neuroscience at Paris Lodron University Salzburg, Austria, investigated the psychological and physiological profile of individuals afflicted by chronic hypnic jerks.

Their findings indicate that recurrent sleep starts are not isolated neuromuscular glitches; rather, they serve as a behavioral manifestation of sleep-related hyperarousal and cognitive-emotional anxiety.

Because standardized psychometric tools for quantifying hypnic jerks have historically been lacking, the research team synthesized existing clinical neurology and sleep medicine literature to construct a targeted assessment battery.

It has been revealed that they surveyed 194 adults across Austria and Germany, dividing them into two cohorts: 96 individuals who experienced abrupt awakenings accompanied by at least one secondary symptom weekly, and 98 matched control participants without frequent sleep starts. Participants completed validated measures assessing insomnia severity, subjective sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, dysfunctional beliefs about sleep, anxiety, and depression.

The resulting symptom profiles revealed that sleep starts involve a multi-sensory and autonomic cascade:.

In a recent development, “Sleep starts are much more than a simple muscle twitch when falling asleep,” explains first author Tanja Grünberger. “Participants described not only jerks, but also sensations of falling, a racing heart, flashes of light or loud bangs, and strong feelings of alarm or fear – and those who reported sleep starts at least once a week also reported poorer sleep quality, more unhelpful beliefs about sleep and more anxiety symptoms.”.

Recent findings suggest that when comparing the two cohorts, the differences were statistically pronounced. Individuals experiencing weekly sleep starts had significantly poorer overall sleep quality, greater insomnia severity, higher levels of general anxiety, elevated depressive symptoms, and more dysfunctional beliefs regarding sleep.

In a recent development, statistical modeling revealed that how frequently people experienced sleep starts was closely tied to sleep quality, rigid sleep beliefs, and anxiety levels. Together with demographic variables (age and gender), these psychological factors accounted for 26.9% of the variance in sleep start frequency between individuals.

Importantly, participants reported that sleep starts surged during periods of psychological distress and emotional strain. In contrast, physical sleep deprivation was less influential on the frequency of episodes.

Industry observers note that “What we found most interesting was how closely sleep starts are linked to how people think and feel about sleep,” Grünberger notes. “The more strongly participants held unhelpful beliefs about sleep and the more anxious they were, the more often they reported sleep starts – and in the moment itself, many described a strong pressure to finally fall asleep. Our data cannot show what causes what, but this pattern resembles what we know from insomnia.”.

Sources indicate that traditional medical advice has often dismissed hypnic jerks as inconsequential physiological quirks requiring no clinical management. However, the Salzburg findings show that for individuals caught in chronic hyperarousal, sleep starts create a self-reinforcing loop: pre-sleep anxiety increases nervous system excitability, triggering a violent startle response, which then reinforces catastrophic beliefs about one’s inability to sleep.

“These findings support the view that sleep starts should be considered within broader frameworks of sleep-related hyperarousal and cognitive-emotional activation,” the authors write.

It has been revealed that looking forward, senior author Manuel Schabus highlights the therapeutic avenues this connection opens: “For most people, sleep starts are a harmless feature of falling asleep. For a subgroup, however, they go along with distress and a longer time to fall asleep. Whether approaches that reduce arousal and sleep-related worry also help with distressing sleep starts has not yet been tested – that is an key next step.”.

Targeted cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), autonomic down-regulation protocols, and pre-sleep relaxation techniques could offer relief for patients whose transition into slumber is repeatedly derailed by their own nervous system.

What are sleep starts or hypnic jerks?

Sleep starts are sudden, involuntary muscle twitches or jolts that occur during the transition from wakefulness to sleep. They can be strong enough to wake a person fully and are often accompanied by sensations of falling, electric shocks, flashes of light, a racing heart, and a sudden surge of fear or alarm.

How do frequent sleep starts relate to mental health and sleep disorders?

People who experience sleep starts at least weekly report significantly worse sleep quality, greater insomnia severity, higher anxiety, and more dysfunctional beliefs about sleep compared to those who do not. The frequency of these jolts tracks closely with daytime emotional strain and psychological stress.

What causes sleep starts to happen more often?

While occasional jerks are normal, frequent episodes appear driven by central nervous system hyperarousal. Heightened stress, performance anxiety around falling asleep, and catastrophic beliefs about insomnia keep the autonomic nervous system on high alert, triggering a startle response instead of a smooth physiological descent into sleep.

Phenomenology and associations with sleep, psychological, and demographic characteristics.

Sleep starts (SS) are transient phenomena during sleep onset. Although traditionally characterized by sudden muscle jerks, they may also involve sensory, cognitive, emotional, and autonomic experiences. Despite their high prevalence, empirical data on phenomenology and associated characteristics remain limited. This online survey examined SS phenomenology and exploratory associations with demographic, sleep-related, and psychological variables in 194 adults.

Sources indicate that participants with self-reported sleep-related movement disorders or relevant medical conditions were excluded. Individuals reporting abrupt awakenings ≥1/week and ≥1 additional symptom formed the SS group (SS frequency ≥1, n = 96); all others the comparison group (SS frequency <1, n = 98). Because SS were operationalized using self-reported symptoms, they could not be distinguished from related sleep-onset phenomena (e.g., exploding head syndrome, hypnagogic hallucinations).

Standardized questionnaires (PSQI, ISI, ESS, MZS, HADS) assessed sleep quality, insomnia severity, daytime sleepiness, dysfunctional sleep-related beliefs, and anxiety/depression symptoms. Participants described diverse experiences including motor jerks, falling sensations, dream-like experiences, somatosensory symptoms, autonomic arousal, and emotional reactions, accompanied by alarm, anxiety, and confusion.

Compared with controls, the SS group reported poorer sleep quality, greater insomnia severity, stronger dysfunctional sleep-related beliefs, and higher anxiety/depressive symptoms (all p < .05). Exploratory regression analyses indicated that poorer sleep quality, stronger dysfunctional sleep-related beliefs, and higher anxiety symptoms were associated with higher SS frequency, whereas depressive symptoms were not. The final model explained 26.9% of variance (R2 = .269, adjusted R2 = .245).

More frequent SS were retrospectively reported during emotional stress, whereas sleep deprivation was perceived as less influential. Although many described SS as manageable, a substantial subgroup reported distress and sleep disruption.

This suggests that SS represent heterogeneous sleep-onset experiences associated with subjective sleep disturbance and cognitive-emotional arousal. Although causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional self-report data, the results highlight potentially relevant links between SS and sleep-related cognitive-emotional processes.

Brain Moves Its Touch Center to Keep Feeling Sensation

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Biomedical engineers at Penn State have solved a major hurdle in neuroprosthetics and sensory rehabilitation: sensory habituation, where the brain gradually stops perceiving continuous artificial electrical stimulation.
  • Recent findings suggest that by delivering 5-second electrical pulse bursts paired with 40-second recovery intervals, the team maintained a stable, unattenuated sensation of touch over 45 minutes across 60 trials.
  • Loss of tactile sensation in the hands, whether resulting from stroke, peripheral nerve injury, spinal trauma, or limb amputation, fundamentally impairs everyday activities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Biomedical engineers at Penn State have solved a major hurdle in neuroprosthetics and sensory rehabilitation: sensory habituation, where the brain gradually stops perceiving continuous artificial electrical stimulation. In a paper published in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, researchers led by Dr. Xiaogang Hu monitored cortical activity using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) during transcutaneous nerve stimulation (TNS).

Recent findings suggest that by delivering 5-second electrical pulse bursts paired with 40-second recovery intervals, the team maintained a stable, unattenuated sensation of touch over 45 minutes across 60 trials. Neuroimaging revealed that while perception remained completely constant, the brain actively distributed tactile processing beyond the primary somatosensory cortex to wider neural networks.

Loss of tactile sensation in the hands, whether resulting from stroke, peripheral nerve injury, spinal trauma, or limb amputation, fundamentally impairs everyday activities. Basic tasks such as holding a fragile ceramic mug, grasping utensils, writing, or typing become daily battles when real-time sensory feedback is absent.

While bioengineers have developed transcutaneous nerve stimulation (TNS) and invasive neural implants capable of delivering artificial electrical pulses to mimic the sensation of touch, these technologies face a universal physiological barrier: sensory habituation.

In a recent development, over extended periods, the central nervous system adapts to repetitive, artificial electrical stimulation. As neural circuits adjust to constant inputs, perceived intensity weakens and eventually fades away entirely. For an amputee using a motorized prosthetic hand, this decay is catastrophic: without steady tactile feedback, an individual cannot regulate grip force, leading them to either crush delicate objects or drop them unexpectedly.

It has been revealed that now, a team of researchers led by Dr. Xiaogang Hu, the Dorothy Foehr Huck and J. Lloyd Huck Chair in Neurorehabilitation and professor of mechanical engineering at Penn State, has uncovered both the neural dynamics of habituation and a stimulation protocol to bypass it.

Published in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, the study demonstrates that finely calibrated stimulation-and-rest intervals can preserve stable, long-term tactile sensations while triggering adaptive redistribution across the brain’s cerebral networks.

Recent findings suggest that “Repetitive stimulation — regardless of whether you engage stimulation through the nerves, skin or directly targeting a part of the brain — will be perceived as declining or weakening over time,” explained Dr. Hu, who holds joint appointments in Penn State’s Departments of Kinesiology and Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation. “With this work, we are trying to avoid or minimize that habituation, enabling a more stable sense of touch over a longer timeframe.”.

To determine how electrical parameters influence neural adaptation, the researchers systematically tested varying electrical pulse durations and resting intervals across healthy volunteers.

Electrodes were placed over peripheral nerves in the forearm to deliver mild electrical pulses designed to feel like a gentle tingling sensation. Using trial-by-trial psychophysical scoring, the team determined that a specific combination, 5 seconds of electrical stimulation followed by a 40-second recovery interval, prevented sensory decay.

When evaluated across an extended 45-minute continuous trial consisting of 60 consecutive stimulation cycles, participants reported zero habituation, retaining a crisp, consistent tactile sensation from the first pulse to the last.

“Picture someone is holding a cup of water with their prosthetic — the sensation of touch is critical for them to maintain an appropriate grip force,” Hu noted. “We don’t want them to crush the cup with too much force or for them to lose their sensation of touch over time and drop the cup; we need to ensure that the feeling is stable.”.

To explore how the brain maintains stable perception during prolonged stimulation, the investigators deployed functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS).

Recent findings suggest that unlike functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which requires patients to lie immobilized inside a massive, noisy scanner bore, fNIRS employs a flexible cap equipped with lightweight optical optodes. These emitters project harmless beams of near-infrared light through the scalp and skull into the superficial cerebral cortex. By measuring how light reflects back to paired photodetectors, the system quantifies local shifts in oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin, serving as a high-fidelity proxy for localized neuronal metabolism and synaptic activity.

Targeting the primary somatosensory cortex (the cerebral hub responsible for mapping bodily touch), fNIRS captured real-time cortical dynamics while participants sat upright and received TNS.

The optical scans uncovered an unexpected neurofunctional divergence: while participants reported that the physical sensation felt identical across all 45 minutes, their underlying brain activation patterns were constantly shifting.

“Participants report that the sensation feels the same, but the active regions in their brain actually change over time, with changing intensity of activation and spatial distribution,” said first author Dr. Susan Coltman, assistant professor at the University of Guelph, who conducted the study as a postdoctoral researcher in Hu’s lab. “The signals start out in the somatosensory cortex, but over time, they move out beyond that origin area to different regions of the brain, reflecting progressive recruitment of distributed brain regions to process information during prolonged sensory stimulation.”.

Rather than a static, local response, sensory preservation appears to depend on the brain dynamically recruiting distributed associative and secondary sensory networks to sustain conscious perception.

These findings carry major implications for clinical neurorehabilitation. Individuals recovering from hemispheric stroke or living with upper-limb amputations already experience extensive cortical reorganization. Understanding how the healthy brain balances stimulation timing and network recruitment provides a quantitative template for programming next-generation bionic prostheses and wearable rehabilitation sleeves.

The research team plans to extend these optimized stimulation paradigms into patient populations with focal stroke lesions and limb loss, aiming to calibrate personalized electrical intervals that accommodate damaged, rewired neural pathways.

By striking the biological balance between stimulation and recovery, engineers are moving closer to artificial limbs that don’t just move naturally, but feel permanently real.

What is sensory habituation in nerve stimulation?

Sensory habituation occurs when the nervous system becomes accustomed to continuous, repetitive artificial electrical stimulation, causing the perceived sensation of touch to gradually weaken and fade away over time.

How did the Penn State team prevent habituation during nerve stimulation?

In a recent development, the researchers identified an optimized timing ratio: applying 5 seconds of mild electrical stimulation followed by a 40-second rest period. This cycle allowed peripheral nerves and central circuits to recover, sustaining a completely stable sense of touch over 45 minutes and 60 cycles.

How did brain activity change during the experiment?

Sources indicate that although participants felt the exact same level of sensation throughout the 45-minute window, fNIRS imaging demonstrated that active brain regions shifted over time. Brain activity originated in the primary somatosensory cortex and then progressively migrated outward, recruiting wider distributed brain networks to sustain sensory processing.

Funding & Support: Supported by the National Institute on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research (NIDILRR) and the U.S. National Science Foundation’s Division of Information and Intelligent Systems (grants IIS-2330862 and IIS-2319139).

fNIRS Characterization of Temporal Potentiation During Optimized Nerve Stimulation.

Restoring stable somatosensory feedback through transcutaneous nerve stimulation (TNS) represents a significant challenge in neural engineering; however, the cortical dynamics underlying sustained stimulation are not yet well characterized.

Industry observers note that this study utilizes a multi-method functional near-infrared spectroscopy framework to quantify the temporal evolution of cortical engagement during temporally structured TNS. It was hypothesized that stimulation parameters fundamentally constrain the spatiotemporal profile of the hemodynamic response function.

A General Linear Model with temporal and dispersion derivatives was used to analyze hemodynamic responses in 10 participants across three phases: validation, duration optimization (2, 5, or 10 seconds), and sustained engagement (45 minutes). During the optimization phase, 5-second stimulation produced the highest canonical amplitude with optimal dispersion characteristics, while 10-second trains resulted in significant temporal delays.

During the sustained phase, parametric modeling indicated no linear decay in cortical response. Instead, the cortex demonstrated temporal potentiation, characterized by a transition from sparse early-phase activation to widespread late-phase recruitment across the sensorimotor network. The left posterior parietal cortex (BA5) served as a continuous integration hub, whereas primary somatosensory regions exhibited dynamic late-onset engagement.

These findings characterize a nonlinear temporal potentiation pattern, demonstrating that the selected stimulation/rest timing regime can sustain cortical engagement and facilitate delayed network expansion. The observed intersubject heterogeneity highlights the necessity for adaptive, closed-loop TNS controllers guided by real-time hemodynamic biomarkers.

#284. High Speed Rail Isn't Just Fast Trains, There Are Rigidly Defined Categories

High Speed Rail Isn't Just Fast Trains, There Are Rigidly Defined Categories

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (440 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The uninformed often fall for the illusion that high-speed rail is simply a railroad operating extremely fast trains.
  • Sources indicate that the FRA defines three tiers of Passenger Equipment Safety Standards delineated by top speed.
  • The agency stipulates that high-speed trains can't travel faster than 160 mph on any track with at-grade crossings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The uninformed often fall for the illusion that high-speed rail is simply a railroad operating extremely fast trains. In actuality, it's an entire transportation system tightly regulated by government agencies. The Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) attempted to spur high-speed rail development in 2018 by letting operators run high-speed trains on existing speed-limited infrastructure, but so far, no latest service has usurped Amtrak's Acela on the Northeast Corridor as America's fastest train. Businesses simply won't buy passenger trains capable of hitting 220 miles per hour if they don't have the dedicated right-of-way needed to reach top speed.

Sources indicate that the FRA defines three tiers of Passenger Equipment Safety Standards delineated by top speed. Each increasing tier requires more stringent crashworthiness, maintenance, and safety standards. Most passenger trains in the United States fall under Tier I, which is limited to 125 mph. Tier II, or higher-speed rail, has a legal top speed of 160 mph. Tier III, established in 2018, allows for speeds up to 220 mph. However, the trains are only half of the equation.

The agency stipulates that high-speed trains can't travel faster than 160 mph on any track with at-grade crossings. Even tracks with a 160 mph limit are rare in the U.S., as the Northeast Corridor has only four short stretches where Acela trains are allowed to touch 160 mph. The rest of the route between Boston and Washington, D.C. is limited to 125 mph. With as many as 386 passengers on board, there can't be any risk of anyone or anything entering the tracks and causing a catastrophic crash.

Japan's Shinkansen is viewed as the archetypal form of high-speed rail. The moniker translates into English as "upcoming main line." Japanese National Railways opened the first Shinkansen line between Tokyo and Osaka in 1964. The five-year construction effort created a new dedicated high-speed main line, separate from commuter and freight traffic on the parallel Tōkaidō Main Line. France's TGV and other high-speed networks in Europe borrowed this dedicated-infrastructure philosophy from the Shinkansen.

Florida's Brightline is the most prominent U.S. example of the failings of shared rights-of-way. The higher-speed service between Miami and Orlando is heavily constrained by its 325-mile route, specifically the portion shared with the Florida East Coast Railway. According to Brightline, its trains are limited to 79 mph along this section. The 67-mile stretch between Miami and West Palm Beach, owned by the freight service, has 156 at-grade crossings. The abundance of crossings creates opportunities for trains to hit vehicles and pedestrians. Brightline-involved collisions have killed over 200 people since 2017. Dedicated rights-of-way are not only faster, they are far safer.

Blood-Brain Barrier Protein Atlas Unlocks Alzheimer’s

💡 Key Takeaways
