  • Industry observers note that in preclinical models of Alzheimer’s disease, researchers discovered that before the barrier physically degrades and leaks toxins, it first shuts down the import of critical protective proteins, such as liver-derived apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1).
  • For more than a century, neuroscientists have viewed the blood-brain barrier (BBB) primarily as a physiological fortress: a tight seal of endothelial cells, pericytes, and astrocytic end-feet designed to keep pathogens, peripheral immune cells, and toxic macromolecules out of delicate cerebral tissue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a study published in Cell, researchers at Gladstone Institutes have created the first comprehensive atlas of circulating blood proteins that cross the blood-brain barrier into the brain. Led by Dr. Andrew Yang, the team deployed Nobel Prize-winning protein-labeling chemistry to track 861 plasma proteins in mice, finding that the blood-brain barrier selectively imports just 92, most originating in distant organs like the liver.

Industry observers note that in preclinical models of Alzheimer’s disease, researchers discovered that before the barrier physically degrades and leaks toxins, it first shuts down the import of critical protective proteins, such as liver-derived apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1). Boosting systemic APOA1 restored neuronal connectivity and halted disease progression, demonstrating that neurodegeneration may begin when the brain’s peripheral molecular supply line is severed.

Source: Gladstone Institutes / Cell.

For more than a century, neuroscientists have viewed the blood-brain barrier (BBB) primarily as a physiological fortress: a tight seal of endothelial cells, pericytes, and astrocytic end-feet designed to keep pathogens, peripheral immune cells, and toxic macromolecules out of delicate cerebral tissue.

However, this fortress model fails to explain how the brain monitors systemic physiology or obtains essential large-molecule signals generated by peripheral organs like the liver and kidneys.

Sources indicate that in a landmark study published in the journal Cell, researchers at Gladstone Institutes overturn this one-way defensive paradigm. Led by Gladstone Investigator Dr. Andrew Yang, the team mapped the first comprehensive atlas of blood-borne proteins transported across the blood-brain barrier into the mammalian brain.

Their findings reveal that the BBB functions as a selective molecular transfer hub, using specialized receptors to sample plasma proteins from distant bodily organs and direct them to specific brain cells using an intrinsic molecular “ZIP code” system.

Critically, the research demonstrates that in Alzheimer’s disease, this supply line breaks down long before the barrier becomes physically porous, opening therapeutic strategies aimed at treating neurodegeneration from the outside in.

Different visceral organs continuously secrete cocktails of signaling proteins into blood plasma to reflect systemic metabolic states. Yet, identifying which of these proteins cross intact cerebral vessels without disrupting normal vascular physiology has historically proven technically impossible.

To solve this, Yang’s team utilized bioorthogonal, click-chemistry protein-labeling strategies to tag the entire mouse plasma proteome without altering biological binding properties.

After infusing labeled plasma proteins back into the circulation of mice, the researchers analyzed cerebral tissue to map which molecules successfully traversed the barrier:.

“We think of blood proteins as messengers carrying signals from distant body parts, and the cells of the blood-brain barrier import only the ones the brain really needs,” explained first author Dr. Haoyue Zhou, a postdoctoral fellow in Yang’s laboratory. “It’s like a molecular ZIP code system that helps each protein reach its intended destination.”.

According to recent reports, A prime example identified in the atlas is apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1). Synthesized predominantly by hepatocytes in the liver, APOA1 travels through the circulation, crosses the BBB, and targets astrocytes. Once bound, it activates signaling cascades required to maintain synaptic density and stabilize neuronal connectivity.

According to recent reports, “For a century, we’ve treated the blood-brain barrier as a simple physical boundary protecting the brain from toxins,” mentioned Dr. Yang, assistant professor of neurology at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) and investigator at Gladstone. “We’re finding that it’s an intelligent interface that plucks the right proteins in the blood, often from distant parts of the body, and delivers them to the right cell types in the brain. Brain health depends on this sophisticated molecular supply line from the body.”.

The team next tracked this transport machinery across the lifespan in mouse models of Alzheimer’s disease.

The prevailing view in neurovascular research holds that Alzheimer’s progression causes the blood-brain barrier to physically disintegrate, opening tight junctions and allowing toxic albumin and fibrinogen to flood the parenchyma, sparking neuroinflammation.

However, Yang and Zhou discovered that an opposing failure occurs first:.

According to recent reports, “Before the barrier starts leaking harmful proteins into the brain, it stops letting the beneficial ones through,” Zhou noted. “The brain’s supply line from the body starts to fail.”.

To test whether replenishing these lost peripheral signals could counteract neurodegeneration, the researchers engineered Alzheimer’s mouse models to overexpress human APOA1 specifically in their liver tissue.

In a recent development, as circulating levels increased, more APOA1 crossed the blood-brain barrier into the central nervous system. The influx of liver-derived APOA1 restored astrocytic support, preserved synaptic connectivity, and reduced cognitive and behavioral signs of Alzheimer’s disease.

“Alzheimer’s disease may not start entirely inside the brain; it may start when the brain’s supply line from the body is severed,” Yang concluded. “If that’s right, we may be able to fight this disease from outside the brain, by restoring what the brain has lost.”.

It has been revealed that the identification of this 92-protein atlas provides dual translational opportunities. First, clinicians could potentially treat cognitive decline by pharmacologically boosting protective protein production in peripheral organs like the liver. Second, by mapping the precise endogenous receptors used by these 92 proteins, bioengineers can design targeted “molecular shuttles” that piggyback life-saving therapeutics across the blood-brain barrier directly to diseased brain cells.

What is the latest blood-brain barrier protein atlas?

Recent findings suggest that it is the first comprehensive molecular catalog of circulating blood proteins that are actively transported across the blood-brain barrier into the brain. Created by Gladstone Institutes researchers, the atlas identifies 92 specific plasma proteins (out of 861 tracked) that cross into the brain, primarily originating in peripheral organs such as the liver.

How does the “molecular ZIP code” system work?

The blood-brain barrier does not allow imported proteins to float around randomly. Once proteins cross the barrier, specialized molecular guidance cues direct them to specific cell types (such as astrocytes, neurons, or microglia) where they perform essential maintenance, such as protecting synaptic connections.

How does this discovery change our understanding of Alzheimer’s disease?

Scientists previously believed the blood-brain barrier’s primary fault in Alzheimer’s was becoming physically leaky. This study shows that before it ever leaks, the barrier stops importing vital protective proteins like APOA1 from the liver. Restoring these peripheral proteins reversed early signs of the disease, proving that neurodegeneration can be combated by repairing the body-to-brain supply line.

Funding: The work was supported by the National Institutes of Health (DP5OD033381), National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (1R01NS128909, 1RF1NS139975), Alzheimer’s Association (ADSF-24-1345199-C), Burroughs Wellcome Fund, the Ludwig Family Foundation, the Dolby Family, UC San Francisco, the Dr. Miriam and Sheldon G. Adelson Medical Research Foundation, the National Institute of General Medical Sciences, the Larry L. Hillblom Foundation (2023-A-020-FEL), the National Science Foundation, and the NOMIS Foundation.

The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through path-ways impaired early in Alzheimer’s disease models.

The blood-brain barrier (BBB) has been defined primarily by what it excludes, yet the scale and function of physiological blood-to-brain protein transport remain largely unknown. Using bioorthogonal proteomics, we find that the healthy BBB samples 191 plasma proteins and permits 92 into the brain parenchyma.

Enriched for carrier and metabolic functions, these proteins home to distinct brain cell types, such as apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) to astrocytes and alpha-1 antitrypsin (SERPINA1) to microglia.

This cell-type tropism relies on a BBB-parenchyma receptor hand-off: APOA1 crosses the BBB via SR-B1 and engages astrocytic ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), a key Alzheimer’s risk gene, driving cholesterol efflux that supports synapse integrity. Unlike LPS-induced nonspecific leakage, early-stage 5xFAD mice show selective BBB transport remodeling, with reduced APOA1 and increased SERPINA1 uptake.

Hepatic APOA1 overexpression restores APOA1 in the 5xFAD brain, rescuing astrocytic, synaptic, and behavioral deficits. These findings recast the BBB as a selective interface that recruits neuroprotective circulatory proteins for brain health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Suzuki X-90 seems to be the only two-seat SUV made for the mass market on a global scale. With that as our influence, we went in search of other two-seat SUVs to find out if they are as stupendously rare as the first appeared. After all, by their very definition, SUVs are supposed to be utilitarian vehicles, and there is nothing practical about a two-seat layout.

In a recent development, if the search were for two-door SUVs, the list might be a little longer and would include the Jeep Wrangler – including the Scrambler SRT Concept. However, even these usually have a rear row of seats, so they do not qualify as a two-seat SUV. And most single-cab pickup trucks are also disqualified, even if an argument can be made that they are SUVs – of a type.

According to recent reports, so back to that little Suzuki of the 1990s. Single-handedly trying to launch a whole new segment of two-seat SUVs, and clearly failing, the X-90 might not seem like it qualifies as a full-blown SUV. After all, it was only 146 inches long and had a 95-horsepower 1.6-liter engine, which are not the normal stats that define an SUV.

In a recent development, but the X-90 did use traditional body-on-frame construction, like proper 4x4s, and also came with four-wheel drive and a live rear axle. Diminutive Suzuki off-roaders have an enviable reputation in the automotive world for going further into the wilderness than their stature suggests, so do not discount the X-90's trail abilities.

It has been revealed that the X-90 was not a hit, though. Its biggest market in the world was the U.S., where only 7,205 found homes in a three-year period from 1996 onwards. So, after the weirdness of the small Suzuki, are there any other vehicles like it out there? Any other two-seat SUVs at all?

Swiss firm Sbarro is known for creating motoring oddities. Among its back catalog are a VW Golf-sized hatchback powered by a Ferrari V8 (though not the one Ducati once built for a Lancia sedan) and an open-topped version of the Renault Espace minivan. But Sbarro also gave us one of the rare two-seat SUVs in the world, in the shape of the Monster G of 1987. This had a spec like no other SUV in history, mainly because the wheels were taken directly from a Boeing 727 airliner.

Sources indicate that other details included an adapted chassis from a Range Rover, a Mercedes 6.3-liter V8 under the hood delivering 350 horsepower, and a folding motorcycle and a portable generator mounted in the trunk of the Monster G. This Sbarro was built as a one-off commission for a wealthy German enthusiast, so you'd be forgiven for not having heard of it.

Industry observers note that in a similar vein, French firm Aixam gave the world another unusual two-seat SUV, in the form of the Mega Track. As a lifted V12-powered supercar – using the engine from the W140 Mercedes S-Class – the Mega Track is more of a precursor to the likes of the Lamborghini Huracan Sterrato and Porsche 911 Dakar than it is a traditional SUV.

The Mega Track was huge, measuring 196.85 inches long and 98.4 inches wide, while also weighing more than 4,400 lb, and it joins the list of rare two-seat SUVs. It also had four-wheel drive and the ability to increase its ground clearance at the press of a button. In comparison to the Sbarro, this car was commonplace, with about five or six vehicles created, but yeah, it's a rare example of a rare genre by any measure.

Following on from the Willys Jeep's use in World War II, it was a logical next step to turn it into a civilian vehicle. Initially, CJ-1 and CJ-2 derivatives were designed primarily as agricultural vehicles that could be used in fields, and by 1945 the CJ-2A was born. This was produced until 1949, and more than 214,000 units were made.

In its most basic form, the CJ-2A wouldn't qualify as a two-seat SUV, as it came with just a driver's seat, although options included a passenger seat and/or a rear bench, so we're adding it to the list. It was possible to remove the rear bench in the original Willys Jeep, of course, turning it into a two-seater. Does anyone consider the Willys Jeep an SUV, though? Probably not.

And while an 80-year-old Jeep may still have the goods, there's a breed of new commercial SUVs in markets across the world which could also qualify as two-seaters, though not many are offered to North American buyers. One example is Toyota's long-serving Land Cruiser, which can trace its origins back to 1951. The current model is sold as a commercial vehicle, and while it looks like the standard civilian station wagon, it in fact has just two seats up front and a mesh ahead of the load area.

Sources indicate that similarly, in some international markets, the current Defender 90 is sold as a commercial vehicle known as the Hard Top, which has just two seats up front. Saying that, Land Rover Classic will restore and "remaster" an old Defender, fitting a 405-horsepower V8 in the process. Among the body styles offered is the "90 Hard Top", which has a two-seat cabin. That, and the "90" part of its name, are about all the Defender shares with the Suzuki X-90.

#280. Autism Shapes How Words vs. Numbers Drive Risk Decisions

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1146 w)
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Neurosciencenews

Autism Shapes How Words vs. Numbers Drive Risk Decisions

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A cognitive psychology study from the University of Tokyo reveals that individuals with and without autism spectrum disorder (ASD) process verbal expressions of probability, such as “likely” or “possible”, through distinctly different decision-making frameworks.
  • Researchers identified three distinct cognitive profiles of decision-makers, discovering that individuals with ASD were heavily swayed by positive or negative verbal framing rather than the underlying numerical probabilities they inferred.
  • Whether weighing the side effects of a latest medication, interpreting climate forecasts, or navigating financial investments, human beings constantly make critical choices based on uncertain information.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A cognitive psychology study from the University of Tokyo reveals that individuals with and without autism spectrum disorder (ASD) process verbal expressions of probability, such as “likely” or “possible”, through distinctly different decision-making frameworks. Published in Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, the research evaluated 138 participants weighing medical treatment recommendations framed in either words or percentages.

Researchers identified three distinct cognitive profiles of decision-makers, discovering that individuals with ASD were heavily swayed by positive or negative verbal framing rather than the underlying numerical probabilities they inferred. The findings underscore the need for clinicians and educators to pair verbal risk estimates with explicit numerical data and interactive dialogue to ensure informed medical decisions.

Whether weighing the side effects of a latest medication, interpreting climate forecasts, or navigating financial investments, human beings constantly make critical choices based on uncertain information. In clinical settings, physicians and educators routinely communicate risk using qualitative verbal descriptors, telling patients a treatment is “likely to succeed” or a side effect is “unlikely”, rather than citing exact statistical percentages.

However, verbal probability terms are inherently ambiguous. One person’s “possible” may translate to a 20% likelihood, while another interprets the exact same word as a 60% chance.

For individuals on the autism spectrum—a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by distinct differences in social communication, pragmatic language processing, and cognitive flexibility, interpreting these imprecise verbal cues presents unique challenges.

In a study published in Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, researchers from the University of Tokyo investigated how adults with and without autism spectrum disorder translate verbal and numerical probabilities into concrete medical decisions.

Led by Hidehito Honda, Hirokazu Kumazaki, and Professor Kazuhiro Ueda from the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, the team uncovered three distinct cognitive profiles governing how people process uncertainty, demonstrating that subtle phrasing choices heavily steer decision-making in autistic individuals.

To evaluate how linguistic framing interacts with statistical reasoning, the researchers recruited 138 adult participants: 48 individuals diagnosed with ASD and 90 neurotypical control participants.

Participants were presented with a realistic clinical decision-making scenario. They were asked to imagine advising a close friend considering an expensive medical treatment for chronic migraines, rating how strongly they would recommend the therapy based on a physician’s prognosis.

Across trials, the doctor’s prognosis was systematically varied across two formats:.

Following the recommendation task, participants were also asked to explicitly translate each verbal expression into a numerical percentage, allowing researchers to separate a person’s internal numerical estimate from the emotional or directional pull of the phrasing itself.

Recent findings suggest that “ASD is often associated with differences in communication and information processing, so we wondered if people with ASD might interpret expressions of uncertainty differently,” explained Professor Kazuhiro Ueda. “While we found that participants with ASD tended to assign more similar numerical meanings to different verbal phrases, we more importantly identified three distinct patterns of decision-making, revealing variation both within and across the groups.”.

When the investigators analyzed how participants weighted wording versus implied numbers, three distinct behavioral clusters emerged:.

The researchers note that because the study sample encompassed a wide range of ages and intellectual abilities, further longitudinal and cognitive testing is required to determine the exact psychological mechanisms—such as differences in pragmatic inference or cognitive load—that place an individual into a specific decision-making cluster.

Nevertheless, the real-world implications for clinical communication are immediate. If a physician describes a 30% success rate as “possible” versus “unlikely,” a framing-sensitive patient may reach opposite treatment conclusions based entirely on word choice rather than clinical reality.

Recent findings suggest that “Even so, our findings suggest that the way we communicate uncertainty deserves more attention, especially when people make crucial decisions about health, education or everyday life. We could see that even subtle differences in wording can influence people’s decisions,” said Ueda.

To ensure genuine informed consent and equitable autonomy, the authors advocate for a shift toward explicit, transparent communication protocols.

Recent findings suggest that “We would like to see greater awareness that communicating uncertainty is not simply a matter of choosing understandable words,” Ueda concluded. “It is important to clearly explain the context and background of the information being provided and to understand which aspects of that information influence each person’s judgments and decisions. We hope our findings will encourage professionals, particularly in healthcare and education, to explain uncertain information more explicitly and check whether their intended meaning has been understood.”.

How do people with autism interpret probability words like “likely” or “possible”?

According to recent reports, the University of Tokyo study found that participants with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) tended to assign more similar numerical percentages across different verbal phrases compared to neurotypical peers. More importantly, when making medical decisions, individuals with ASD were far more influenced by whether a phrase was framed positively or negatively rather than the underlying numerical probability.

What are the three types of decision-makers identified in the study?

Researchers identified three cognitive profiles: Group 1 (mostly individuals with ASD), who rely heavily on positive or negative wording; Group 2 (mostly neurotypical adults), who base choices primarily on inferred numerical probabilities; and Group 3 (a mix of both groups), who weigh wording and numbers equally.

How should doctors and educators communicate risk based on these findings?

Professionals should avoid relying solely on vague verbal terms like “possible” or “unlikely.” Instead, they should provide clear numerical percentages alongside explicit context, and engage in two-way dialogue to verify that the patient or student has understood the intended meaning.

Funding: This research was supported by Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research (Grant Numbers JP22H03911 and JP25H01131).

Understanding verbal and numerical probability information and decision-making among individuals with and without autism spectrum disorder.

This study examined how individuals with and without autism spectrum disorder (ASD) interpret probabilistic information expressed verbally or numerically, and how such interpretations influence decision-making.

Two experiments were conducted: Experiment 1 included 48 participants with ASD and 41 participants without ASD in the final analyses, and Experiment 2 included an independent sample of 49 participants without ASD. Participants translated verbal probability expressions (e.g., likely, doubtful) into numerical estimates and made hypothetical treatment recommendations based on either verbal or numerical probabilities.

According to recent reports, compared with non-ASD individuals, participants with ASD showed less differentiated numerical translations across verbal probability expressions, indicating greater similarity in the numerical meanings assigned to different expressions. A hierarchical Bayesian analysis followed by cluster analysis identified three decision-making profiles.

Notably, individuals with ASD were more likely to belong to a cluster characterized by stronger sensitivity to the directionality (positive vs. negative framing) of verbal probability expressions and weaker reliance on numerical translation. In contrast, non-ASD individuals were more frequently represented in a cluster that relied primarily on numerical information.

These findings suggest that individuals with and without ASD differ in how verbal probability expressions are interpreted and incorporated into decision making, highlighting the importance of considering individual differences in the communication of uncertainty.

#278. Breaking: How F1 Transmissions Can Select Two Gears At Once And Keep Racing For 3,000 Miles

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (847 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

Breaking: How F1 Transmissions Can Select Two Gears At Once And Keep Racing For 3,000 Miles

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there's a bit of madness required to craft F1 cars, let alone drive them.
  • It has been revealed that and an F1 shift happens in as little as 2 milliseconds, versus the leisurely 100 milliseconds it takes a dual-clutch transmission to shift in a supercar.
  • The reason it doesn't is that the gearbox can transfer load so rapidly that it's nearly in two gears simultaneously — but not exactly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there's a bit of madness required to craft F1 cars, let alone drive them. The transmissions have to be able to absorb 3,800 shifts per race, and ideally last at least half the season — because they cost roughly $330,000. However, they're now so reliable, despite enduring tremendous forces, that a prior regulation that restricted each team to five transmissions a season was dropped. Ferrari has remarked its gearbox can survive for over 3,000 miles without any issues. That's thousands and thousands of gear changes, and just about a whole Formula 1 season.

It has been revealed that and an F1 shift happens in as little as 2 milliseconds, versus the leisurely 100 milliseconds it takes a dual-clutch transmission to shift in a supercar. That's a tenth of a second for the street sports car versus a 500th of a second for the F1 car, or 50 times faster per shift. Your mind should melt at that figure — and so, you'd think, would an F1 gearbox.

The reason it doesn't is that the gearbox can transfer load so rapidly that it's nearly in two gears simultaneously — but not exactly. The key here is mechanical. A device called a dog ring handles gear swaps. Through a simple revision of the shape of the ring's teeth, engineers were able to make the dog rings do two jobs at once — grab a gear when one side of its teeth are pushed against it, and if the driver selects another gear, the change in rpm forces the first ring to disengage. The fact that the change happens so rapidly is necessary both to prevent double-gear engagement. Simultaneously, this gives teams a critical advantage that's become the motivating force behind F1's transmission arms race.

There were multiple reasons to ditch the manual gearbox in F1. First, if you're toggling a stick-shift gearbox you have to manipulate a clutch with your left foot, which makes it tougher to brake simultaneously. And it means you have to take one hand off the wheel to perform the gear change.

Sources indicate that but Ferrari wasn't concerned about the added stress on its drivers when it pioneered paddle-shifting in 1989. Instead, it was chasing aerodynamic efficiency, and the mechanical linkages at the front of the brand's F1 car made it bulkier than if you could eliminate these elements. Which is what Ferrari did, switching to a hydraulic system controlled electronically each time the driver flipped a paddle. While the transmission was a reliability nightmare during its debut season, by 1990 Ferrari was winning with it.

Industry observers note that that led to a development war, and by 1993 Williams engineered an even more advanced Continuously Variable Transmission, or CVT, which was banned before it could even compete. Yes, we know your CVT hate is way overblown and bordering on irrational. But Williams' CVT wasn't the widget you're envisioning. Instead, it was the precursor to today's ultra-reliable gearbox, and it could keep an F1 car's engine on the boil, never dropping rpm — exactly the advantage of the modern F1 transmission.

According to recent reports, while Williams' 1990s CVT was banned, the modern F1 gearbox that enables 2-millisecond shifts has fundamentally the same result, maintaining constant power output and shaving crucial nanoseconds between gear swaps. All of those hundredths of a second over thousands of shifts add up to over 10 seconds of advantage during the course of an entire race.

According to recent reports, none of the trickery that enables such fast shifts would matter if it didn't come concurrently with advances in material science. Teams are 3D-printing titanium, then carving out small sections of that titanium and replacing them with carbon fiber to further reduce weight. Then F1 squads use a coating process on some parts called diamond-like carbon to reduce parts friction and increase wear life. All of these materials have to be used to withstand punishing heat while still offering exceptional strength-to-weight ratios.

That hand crafting as well as the gearbox's exotic materials explain its extreme cost. Still, that's a mere third of a million bucks, which is nothing compared to the $10 million to $15 million price of an entire F1 engine — even though they don't last long.

Probably what's more amazing about the transmission is that it's a stressed member. That means the gearbox not only has to withstand all the forces of constant rpm at up to 15,000 rpm and 500th-of-a-second gear changes, but it's also supporting the entire rear crash structure as well as the suspension. And the gearbox weighs a mere 88 pounds.

Sources indicate that on top of all of that, F1 cars get a trick differential that's similar to what you'd want for your 4x4, since it can lock both rear wheels together in an instant to enable faster take-off. We'll suggest you might want to know the difference between a fully locking rear diff and a limited-slip differential before you decide to pavement-launch your not-F1 street car and detonate its non-3D-printed parts into smithereens.

#277. 3D Genome Atlas Reveals Early Roots of Schizophrenia

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1340 w)

3D Genome Atlas Reveals Early Roots of Schizophrenia

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1340 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in a landmark study published in Cell, an NIH BRAIN Initiative consortium co-led by UCLA neuroscientists has mapped the molecular and 3D genomic development of the human basal ganglia from mid-pregnancy through infancy.
  • The atlas revealed that spiny projection neurons mature in a highly coordinated manner early in gestation and carry strong enrichment for genetic variants linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, establishing an unprecedented developmental reference to pinpoint when and where psychiatric risk takes root.
  • It has been revealed that during fetal development, the human brain undergoes an extraordinary cellular migration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in a landmark study published in Cell, an NIH BRAIN Initiative consortium co-led by UCLA neuroscientists has mapped the molecular and 3D genomic development of the human basal ganglia from mid-pregnancy through infancy. Analyzing nearly 287,000 individual brain cells using advanced single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing, researchers tracked how developing neurons migrate from temporary prenatal structures known as the ganglionic eminences.

The atlas revealed that spiny projection neurons mature in a highly coordinated manner early in gestation and carry strong enrichment for genetic variants linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, establishing an unprecedented developmental reference to pinpoint when and where psychiatric risk takes root.

It has been revealed that during fetal development, the human brain undergoes an extraordinary cellular migration. Newly born neurons arise in transient, specialized germinal zones and travel long distances across developing tissue to assemble into functional circuits.

Because many of these temporary prenatal structures vanish around the time of birth, capturing the molecular transformations that unfold during this migration has historically been one of neurobiology’s greatest technical challenges.

One critical destination for these migrating cells is the basal ganglia, a deep cluster of subcortical nuclei governing motor control, habit formation, reward processing, and behavioral regulation. Dysfunction within basal ganglia circuitry is implicated across a broad spectrum of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Parkinson’s disease, Huntington’s disease, addiction, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and schizophrenia.

Now, in a study published in the journal Cell, a multi-institutional research team co-led by scientists at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), UC San Francisco, and UC San Diego has mapped the developmental trajectory of the human basal ganglia from mid-pregnancy through infancy in unprecedented 3D molecular detail.

Conducted as part of the National Institutes of Health’s BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN), the study establishes a foundational reference atlas showing how gene regulation and physical DNA folding orchestrate human brain maturation—and how inherited genetic risk for psychiatric disorders maps onto specific developing cell types.

While standard single-cell atlases primarily catalog which genes are actively transcribed, they often miss the upstream epigenetic mechanisms that dictate when and where genes are switched on or off.

According to recent reports, to uncover these regulatory blueprints, co-senior authors Dr. Chongyuan Luo and Dr. Jason Ernst of UCLA, alongside co-leads Dr. Mercedes Paredes (UCSF) and Dr. Eran Mukamel (UCSD), focused on the ganglionic eminences—transient prenatal brain structures that generate the majority of the brain’s inhibitory interneurons as well as key projection neurons destined for the basal ganglia.

Sources indicate that “Genetic studies can tell us that particular regions of the genome are associated with disease, but they often can’t tell us which cell type is affected or when during development that genetic risk becomes relevant,” explained Luo, associate professor of human genetics at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA and member of the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center. “This atlas gives us that cellular and developmental context.”.

Sources indicate that “Because these structures disappear around birth, adult brain studies miss an key early part of these neurons’ development,” added co-first author Matthew Heffel, a former doctoral researcher in Luo’s laboratory. “By sampling them directly, we can compare cells near where they originate with related cells after they have migrated to other parts of the brain.”.

Recent findings suggest that deploying a specialized technique co-developed by Luo’s team called single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), the investigators simultaneously measured DNA methylation patterns and the physical three-dimensional folding of chromatin inside more than 155,000 individual cell nuclei collected from nine developing human brains spanning mid-pregnancy to seven months postnatally. Integrating these profiles with existing developmental and adult datasets brought the total analytical atlas to nearly 287,000 cells.

The expanded single-cell atlas revealed that neural populations arising from distinct subregions of the ganglionic eminences mature on sharply divergent biological schedules. While certain neuronal lineages achieved relative molecular maturity by mid-pregnancy, other progenitor pools continued generating immature neurons well into postnatal infancy.

Among these populations, spiny projection neurons, the primary output neurons of the basal ganglia, stood out. Unlike neighboring neural subtypes, spiny projection neurons matured in a highly synchronized, coordinated wave, exhibiting molecular signatures of functional neuronal activity as early as mid-pregnancy. This early activation suggests they actively participate in wiring basal ganglia circuits long before birth.

Industry observers note that postnatally, the atlas also captured a dramatic genomic restructuring event within oligodendrocytes—the glial support cells responsible for wrapping nerve fibers in insulating myelin sheaths. As immature oligodendrocyte progenitor cells differentiated into mature myelinating oligodendrocytes after birth, their nuclear DNA temporarily folded into a distinct 3D chromatin configuration directly linked to heightened transcriptional activity.

To translate this basic developmental map into clinical insight, the researchers integrated their 3D epigenomic atlas with large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of major psychiatric disorders.

The analysis demonstrated that developing spiny projection neurons harbor an exceptionally strong enrichment for genetic risk variants tied to schizophrenia, with specific subtypes also showing significant associations with bipolar disorder.

It has been revealed that because the study evaluated neurotypical developing tissue rather than patient samples, the findings do not indicate that these neurons directly cause schizophrenia. Rather, the atlas narrows down the exact cellular and developmental windows during which inherited genetic variations may alter circuit assembly.

“Researchers can compare what they see in patients or disease models with typical development to identify the cell types and molecular features that may be most relevant to disease,” noted co-senior author Jason Ernst, UCLA professor of biological chemistry, computer science, and computational medicine.

By providing an open, high-resolution epigenetic and 3D genomic reference of human brain assembly, the BICAN basal ganglia atlas equips neuroscientists with a vital tool to decode the developmental origins of neuropsychiatric illness.

What is the basal ganglia, and why did researchers map its development?

Sources indicate that the basal ganglia is a group of deep brain structures essential for controlling movement, habits, reward, and behavior, and it is heavily implicated in conditions like Parkinson’s disease, addiction, OCD, and schizophrenia. Researchers mapped its development from mid-pregnancy to infancy to capture critical molecular changes in transient prenatal brain structures that disappear around birth.

How did this study differ from previous brain cell atlases?

While most brain atlases simply measure which genes are turned on or off, this study used single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq) across nearly 287,000 cells to simultaneously map DNA methylation and how DNA physically folds in 3D space inside individual cell nuclei, revealing how gene regulation is controlled during cell migration and maturation.

How does this atlas connect to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder?

When researchers overlaid genetic risk variants from large psychiatric studies onto their developmental map, they discovered that developing spiny projection neurons in the basal ganglia were strongly enriched for genetic variants linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, helping pinpoint when and where inherited risk acts during early brain assembly.

Funding: The study was co-led by Dr. Mercedes Paredes of UC San Francisco and Eran Mukamel of UC San Diego and was funded by the NIH, with additional support from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative.

A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia.

Human basal ganglia (BG) neurons and inhibitory interneurons originate in the ganglionic eminences (GEs), transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain.

This study delineates the specification and maturation of GEs and GE-derived neurons using single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and single-molecule chromatin + RNA imaging, and we found heterogeneous temporal progression across GE subregions.

Spiny projection neurons (SPNs), the principal cells of the BG, acquire distinct subtypes through synchronized 3D-epigenomic remodeling, in contrast to the asynchronous maturation of other neuron types.

Oligodendrocyte differentiation involves a transient short-range chromatin state during infancy, showing that the short-range and long-range chromatin conformations previously linked to terminal glial and neuronal fates can also be transient. The temporal cortex matured epigenomically faster than other cortical regions during this period.

It has been revealed that lastly, SPNs were enriched in genetic risk for neuropsychiatric disease. Our study extends findings on unique 3D-epigenomic dynamics during human brain development.

#274. Breaking: Irregular Sleep Schedules Tied to Depression & Loneliness

Breaking: Irregular Sleep Schedules Tied to Depression & Loneliness

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A large-scale wearable data study reveals that erratic daily sleep and wake times are strongly linked to worse depression, anxiety, and loneliness.
  • While public health messaging traditionally emphasizes logging seven to nine hours of sleep per night, emerging chronobiology research indicates that when you sleep may be just as vital to mental well-being as how long you sleep.
  • Erratic bedtimes and fluctuating wake schedules disrupt the body’s internal master clock, throwing off downstream biological rhythms that govern hormone secretion, body temperature, and emotional regulation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A large-scale wearable data study reveals that erratic daily sleep and wake times are strongly linked to worse depression, anxiety, and loneliness. The analysis of 23,000 adults over five months found that progressive declines in sleep regularity weaken circadian alignment and correspond with escalating psychiatric symptoms.

While public health messaging traditionally emphasizes logging seven to nine hours of sleep per night, emerging chronobiology research indicates that when you sleep may be just as vital to mental well-being as how long you sleep.

Erratic bedtimes and fluctuating wake schedules disrupt the body’s internal master clock, throwing off downstream biological rhythms that govern hormone secretion, body temperature, and emotional regulation.

In a large-scale digital health investigation published in Scientific Reports, neuroscientists and behavioral researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) and UC San Diego (UCSD) examined months of continuous biometric data from roughly 23,000 adults.

Led by first author Dr. Severine Soltani and senior author Dr. Ashley Mason, the study reveals that progressive sleep irregularity is directly tied to elevated rates of severe depression, clinical anxiety, and social loneliness.

According to recent reports, previous investigations into sleep regularity have largely relied on subjective sleep diaries or brief, one-week actigraphy snapshots. To capture long-term physiological dynamics, the research team analyzed biometric telemetry from participants enrolled in TemPredict, a nationwide study debuted in 2020 that utilized Oura smart rings to monitor movement and vital signs.

Participants (mean age 46) contributed an average of 154 days of continuous sleep recordings alongside monthly validated mental health surveys evaluating depression, anxiety, and loneliness. From the smart-ring timestamps, investigators computed each individual’s Sleep Regularity Index (SRI), a 0-to-100 metric quantifying day-to-day consistency in sleep onset and wake timing, where higher scores denote stricter schedule adherence.

When the team compared their multi-month dataset against simulated “typical week” snapshots, they discovered that the links between erratic sleep timing and psychological distress were substantially stronger over the long term.

“Regular sleep and wake time help keep circadian rhythms aligned,” explained senior author Dr. Ashley Mason, associate professor in the UCSF Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and affiliate at the UCSF Osher Center for Integrative Health. “Irregular sleep-wake timing may weaken circadian alignment, which is associated with depression and other mental health disorders.”.

Across the 23,000-person cohort, lower Sleep Regularity Index scores tracked closely with escalating psychiatric symptom severity:.

“Someone with an SRI of 84 might go to bed and wake up roughly an hour earlier or later than the previous day, on average,” noted first author Dr. Severine Soltani, formerly of the Bioinformatics and Systems Biology graduate program at UC San Diego. “For someone with an SRI of 75, that shift in sleep schedule might be closer to an hour and a half.”.

Beyond internal circadian desynchrony, Mason pointed out that shifting wake times destabilize daily behavioral anchors—altering exposure to morning sunlight, meal timing, physical exercise, and social engagement, all of which act as critical zeitgebers (time-givers) that stabilize mood circuits.

Because the dataset captures observational correlations across time, the researchers note that the relationship between erratic sleep and mood disorders is likely bidirectional: while depression and anxiety frequently fragment sleep architecture, unstable sleep schedules also actively erode emotional resilience.

“Other longitudinal research provides some reason to think that irregular sleep may come first and contribute to later poor health, rather than being solely a consequence of it,” Mason mentioned.

It has been revealed that by demonstrating that even a 30-to-60-minute increase in daily schedule drift separates healthy individuals from those experiencing severe psychiatric symptoms, the findings highlight a concrete, modifiable behavioral target. Future clinical trials will test whether structured circadian stabilization interventions, anchoring consistent wake times and morning light exposure, can serve as scalable adjunct therapies to alleviate depression, anxiety, and loneliness.

What is the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI), and how does it relate to mental health?

The Sleep Regularity Index measures how consistently a person goes to sleep and wakes up at the exact same times from day to day on a scale of 0 to 100. The study found that lower scores (indicating more erratic sleep schedules) correlate with progressively worse symptoms of depression, anxiety, and loneliness.

How much does a sleep schedule have to vary to link to severe depression?

Individuals with no depressive symptoms averaged an SRI of 84, which corresponds to roughly a 1-hour average daily shift in bed and wake times. Those with severe depressive symptoms averaged an SRI of 75, corresponding to an average daily schedule shift closer to 1.5 hours.

Why does an irregular sleep schedule affect mood and loneliness?

Recent findings suggest that inconsistent sleep and wake times weaken the body’s internal circadian rhythm. Beyond biological misalignment, fluctuating schedules disrupt daily anchors such as morning sunlight exposure, meal timing, physical activity, and opportunities for regular social connection.

According to recent reports, funding: Medical Technology Enterprise Consortium (MTEC) and the U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command (USAMRDC) under the U.S. Department of Defense. Also #StartSmall Foundation and Oura Health Oy.

Associations between sleep regularity indexed from wearable device data and mental health symptoms in the TemPredict longitudinal cohort study.

It has been revealed that the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) is an emerging sleep metric associated with health outcomes. We tested whether SRI derived from wearable device data correlated with self-reported depression, anxiety, and loneliness symptoms cross-sectionally in the TemPredict Study (N = 22,894).

Sources indicate that we computed SRI using all available days with sufficient data (All Days) and a 7-day period before COVID-related restrictions (Typical Week). We used t-tests to compare SRI across mental health severity categories and logistic regression to estimate odds of worse severity before and after covariate adjustment.

Industry observers note that lower SRI was associated with greater depression, anxiety, and loneliness severity in a graded pattern. In All Days analyses, mean SRI was lower among participants with severe depression (74.93 vs. 83.74; p<.0001), severe anxiety (78.94 vs. 83.67; p<.0001), and elevated loneliness (81.79 vs. 83.75; p<.0001) than within normal limits.

It has been revealed that standardized effect sizes comparing SRI in participants with mild/moderate/severe mental health symptoms to those within normal limits were − 0.18 to -1.32 (depression), -0.13 to -0.69 (anxiety), and − 0.27 (loneliness). Logistic models showed greater odds of greater symptom severity per 5-point SRI decrease. Results were similar for Typical Week analyses.

Sleep regularity metrics derived from wearable devices may represent modifiable risk factors to be evaluated in intervention studies.

#273. Tech Report: Are Collectors Overpaying For These Japanese Sports Cars?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2005 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

Tech Report: Are Collectors Overpaying For These Japanese Sports Cars?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you've been paying close attention to the collector car market in recent years, particularly since 2020, you've likely noticed that many golden era Japanese cars have started going for major bucks.
  • Recent findings suggest that considering the comparative mass-market production numbers of some of these Japanese classics, maybe there isn't enough rarity for these cars to command the numbers they do.
  • At the end of the day, cars are only worth what someone is willing to pay for them, and in each of these cases it seems there are plenty of people willing to spend what it takes to buy them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've been paying close attention to the collector car market in recent years, particularly since 2020, you've likely noticed that many golden era Japanese cars have started going for major bucks. Wealthy Gen X and millennial enthusiasts are pushing this nostalgia-fueled, Gran Turismo-inspired market well past what anyone might have thought possible in years gone by. With six-figure price tags no longer out of the ordinary, perhaps it's time to put a finger on the market's pulse and dig into the forces driving these massive prices. Are these cars really worth the spend, and will they continue to hold value into the future? It's tough to say for sure, but I'll give it my best shot.

Recent findings suggest that considering the comparative mass-market production numbers of some of these Japanese classics, maybe there isn't enough rarity for these cars to command the numbers they do. Then again, these are some of the greatest cars of their eras, and no automaker on the planet makes anything today that can compete on a level playing ground with the best of years gone by. Perhaps these values are just a combination of "They just don't make them like they used to" and "They aren't making any more of them.".

At the end of the day, cars are only worth what someone is willing to pay for them, and in each of these cases it seems there are plenty of people willing to spend what it takes to buy them. Surely there are plenty of fools quick to part with their money, and there always will be. Some of these premium prices, however, are getting out of hand. Let's pump the brakes a little and get realistic about what collectors are actually getting for their cash.

I've spilled plenty of ink and burned plenty of internet pixels extolling the virtues of the flip-up-headlight Acura NSX. This is an incredible car and the driving experience is sublime. Perhaps the only problem with the NSX, especially now that Acura has started to reproduce many of the components needed to keep one alive, is that it's too good. The NSX doesn't have the sound or the fizz many of its Italian or German competitors from the era do. In that respect it's perhaps a little on the sterile side. It's so well-engineered that it just does everything you expect it to, which can't always be said of those competitors.

The long and short of this car is that I love it dearly, and I kind of understand why people are willing to spend deep into the hundreds of thousands of dollars for one. According to Hagerty, a #1 conscours-condition car is valued at a quarter of a million on the high end. This is borne out in recent Bring A Trailer auction results, with 10 red first-gen NSXes selling in October alone, ranging from $72,000 on up to $156,000 for a low-mile example. In many cases that's on par with, or even more than, Bring A Trailer's current sales prices of its contemporary Ferrari 348 competitors.

Between 1991 and the end of NSX production in 2004, U.S. sales added up to 8,733 cars, and about 18,000 worldwide. That's actually quite rare, all things considered, but there are always a few available. Buy a high-mile driver-grade NSX at a discount and keep driving it. These things are best once they've worn in a little.

In a recent development, when Datsun debuted the 240Z in the late 1960s as a bargain-priced competitor to the premium European sports cars of the day, it was wildly successful and helped cement the brand's place in the U.S. market. Why spend so much more for a Porsche 911 when a Datsun offered a similar level of performance and head-turning good looks? All these decades later, the 240Z is still a great low-priced vintage alternative to a vintage 911. Today the price gap is perhaps even higher between the German and the Datsun, though the maintenance and aftermarket parts support for both has continued to narrow.

Hagerty claims a #1 condition 240Z will command up to $181,000 at auction, but I don't think anything near that is even close to accurate. I've seen perfectly restored examples trade hands recently for as little as $50,000, and driver-grade units sell on Bring A Trailer every couple of weeks for between 20 and 45 grand. Whatever your budget, and whatever your stomach for tinkering, there's a 240Z out there for you.

Between 1969 and 1973 Nissan shipped 168,584 of these great little machines around the world. The vast majority of them (nearly 90%) ended up in the U.S., largely due to Europe's restrictive post-World War II trade embargoes. It's hard to call a 240Z overpriced, simply by dint of how many were built. There are plenty out there to sate collector demand, and prices reflect that. If you want one, go for it. As with any old car, beware of rusty, poorly restored cars, or any with a checkered past, as you'll pay more to fix one with complications than the premium for a nice one.

Industry observers note that I am a Honda S2000 sycophant, convinced that this is the best driving experience that money can buy. If the Mazda Miata is always the answer, then the S2000 is the path to enlightenment. The early cars with an 8,800-rpm-redline 2.0-liter four-cylinder are pure driving joy. This is exhilaration, verve, and direct feel distilled to its most pure and uncut. If you've never driven one, you'll never understand it. Unlike the NSX, the S2000 is all fizz and very little usability. It's not great on the highway, isn't particularly comfortable, and has no room for anything. It was built to make you feel something, and that's pretty much all it can do. It's a real one-trick pony, but that trick is sublime.

In a recent development, hagerty pegs a perfect condition AP1 at just over $64,000, up 22% from three years ago. Real-world sales on Bring A Trailer show buyers tapping out at $50,000 on the high end, with nice driver-grade examples down in the low 20s. If you look you might be able to find some in the high teens.

Sources indicate that it's hard to call the S2000 rare, as Honda built over 110,000 of these little screamers across 11 years of production. I prefer the models built from 1999 to 2003; they're a little lighter, rev higher and the handling is more like balancing on the edge of a knife. Honda built far more AP1 versions of the car than it did the later 2.2-liter AP2 models, as 72,684 of the former made it out into the world. I don't think these will ever be purely collectible, just on the sheer number built, so don't pay a premium for a #1 example. Buy a nice driver and enjoy miles on twisty roads and track days.

As enthusiastic as I am about Honda's ripper S2000, I remain perplexed by the stratospheric growth of JZA80 Toyota Supra Turbo love. Aside from its role as the star of "The Fast And The Furious" and some highly modified examples, it's an entirely underwhelming ownership experience. Toyota designed the fourth-generation Supra around subframes, suspension, and drivetrain assemblies from the Z30-generation Soarer (sold in the U.S. as the Lexus SC), meaning it's a highly competent, comfortable grand tourer, but a sports car it is not. If you're after a high-speed long-legged highway cruiser, it's pretty great, but it doesn't really feel special to drive.

There's something to be noted for above-average ergonomics and a practically indestructible engine wrapped in simple, attractive bodywork? Of course, but is it a driving experience worth up to $297,000? According to Hagerty, a concours condition Supra could bring that sum at auction. I can't recall having seen one trade hands for quite that much recently, but there are plenty of examples deep into the six figures, like this low-mile unit that went unsold on Bring A Trailer after a high bid of $209,000.

Sources indicate that in every case I'd personally rather have a C5-generation Corvette, offering more power and more twisty-road-ready driving character for orders of magnitude less money. I'm excited that Japanese cars have been grabbing collector attention for the last couple of decades, but I'm positive you can find better cars offering more excitement behind the wheel than this. Japan, and indeed Toyota, has built better grand tourers and better sports cars (and cars that are better at both) since this car exited production.

The Acura Integra Type R is perhaps the car that best exemplifies the overpriced Japanese collector car. Don't get me wrong, this is a magnificent machine with legendary driving character, but at its core it's a pumped-up economy car. Even though it's possibly the best front-wheel-drive experience, and punches well above its weight, it seems downright offensive that these occasionally command six- figure price tags. It's got all the incredible characteristics of a fast Honda, including the reliability, tight steering, and wonderful shifter feel. It also comes with the downsides of a loud, buzzy interior, aesthetically underwhelming design, and a lack of low-end torque. It's a lot of fun on a track or a twisty road, but not a very nice daily driving experience.

Recent findings suggest that according to the Hagerty valuation tool, an Integra Type R in concours condition can expect to bring around $99,000 at auction on the high end. This one seems to actually be underselling the highs of the Integra market, as Bring a Trailer results show. Last summer a low-mile ITR traded hands for $204,204. While nothing has reached that high since, a 19,000-mile example sold for $88,500 in October. Many of these cars have a checkered past, as Integras were once the most stolen car in America, so if you find one with high miles or a rebuilt title, you can probably get the same driving experience for a major discount. A driver-grade car seems to sell in the $20,000-to-$30,000 range.

If you're looking for a less expensive high-revving, great-handling front-wheel-drive economy-based car that works great when the road gets curvy, maybe try a Dodge Neon ACR instead. I put my money where my mouth is a couple years ago, and I never had any ITR jealousy.

There are plenty of other cars from Japan in this conversation, but I don't think this is an intrinsically Japanese collector car problem. In fact, cars from Japan tend to be overlooked by collectors, and have been for decades. There are plenty of reasons to buy a Japanese sports car, but as the market continues to trend upward, many enthusiasts are getting priced out of their dream cars. Still, some, perhaps even many, Japanese cars are still worth the money they command on the used market, especially in light of the lack of choices and driver connectivity in the upcoming car market.

According to recent reports, I typically don't like to talk about collector car values, because it continues to prop up the cars-as-commodities trading industry. Buy what you love and what makes you feel good, and drive the wheels off the thing. What's the point in having a car if you aren't going to drive it as it was meant to be driven? You don't get emotion or experience from storing value in your garage. Perhaps more than any other car-building nation, Japan understands experience and the interconnectedness between driver and machine.

It has been revealed that if you're buying one of these cars because you're expecting it to go up in value and make you money, perhaps you'd be better served investing in the stock market or betting on the ponies. Cars are passion and craftsmanship, and they need to be driven to extract their full value to humanity. Go to a car show, a track day, or take one on a long road trip with friends. There are smiles to be found in those miles. Buy what makes you happy.

Hidden Body Map in Brain Explains Complex Coordination

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Neuroscientists discovered a previously hidden full-body map within the secondary motor cortex (M2), a brain region long thought to lack somatotopic organization.
  • Coordinating the simultaneous motion of an arm, hand, head, and lips to sip a spoonful of soup feels effortless to the human brain, yet executing such fluid multi-part actions remains one of the most formidable challenges in robotics and computational neuroscience.
  • For decades, neuroscientists have understood that the primary motor cortex (M1) contains an orderly somatotopic “body map”, a spatial arrangement in which distinct cortical zones control individual muscles and body parts, such as a single finger or toe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neuroscientists discovered a previously hidden full-body map within the secondary motor cortex (M2), a brain region long thought to lack somatotopic organization. The study used high-speed wide-field optical imaging to analyze resting-state brain activity in mice, revealing synchronized sub-regions linking M2 to the sensory cortex that activate during complex, multi-limb actions.

Coordinating the simultaneous motion of an arm, hand, head, and lips to sip a spoonful of soup feels effortless to the human brain, yet executing such fluid multi-part actions remains one of the most formidable challenges in robotics and computational neuroscience.

For decades, neuroscientists have understood that the primary motor cortex (M1) contains an orderly somatotopic “body map”, a spatial arrangement in which distinct cortical zones control individual muscles and body parts, such as a single finger or toe.

However, direct electrical stimulation of the neighboring secondary motor cortex (M2) yielded ambiguous results, leading researchers to conclude that M2 lacked a structured body map and instead operated purely as an abstract motor planning center.

In a recent development, now, in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers led by Dr. Weihao Xu and Dr. Elizabeth Hillman at Columbia’s Mortimer B. Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute have overturned that assumption.

Using advanced wide-field optical neuroimaging, the team discovered a complete, previously hidden body map embedded within the resting-state neural activity of M2, revealing how the brain integrates sensory feedback to orchestrate complex, multi-limb movements.

Studying motor control in mice poses a unique experimental hurdle because rodents rarely move a single body part in isolation. Rather than relying solely on artificial electrical stimulation or isolated movement tasks, Dr. Xu and colleagues utilized high-speed wide-field optical imaging techniques pioneered in the Hillman laboratory to capture cortex-wide neural dynamics in real time.

Unexpectedly, the critical breakthrough emerged not while the mice were actively moving, but while they were completely at rest. By analyzing spontaneous, seemingly random neural fluctuations across the resting cortex, the investigators spotted localized patches within M2 whose firing patterns synchronized precisely with established body-part sub-regions in the sensory cortex.

Recent findings suggest that “We put these small spots together, and found that they formed a body map hidden in the intrinsic chatter of M2, a part of the brain that wasn’t supposed to have a body map,” noted lead author Dr. Weihao Xu, who conducted the research as a doctoral student and postdoctoral scientist in Hillman’s lab.

To ensure these signals were not bleeding over from neighboring M1, Xu spent three years validating the finding using two-color wide-field optical mapping. By optically separating corticospinal projection neurons (which concentrate heavily in M1 and send direct commands down the spinal cord) from surrounding cortical populations, the team confirmed that the newly mapped zones resided squarely within M2.

Anatomical circuit tracing further confirmed that each sub-region of the newfound M2 body map maintained direct structural wiring with its corresponding counterpart in the sensory cortex.

When the researchers monitored these exact M2 zones during active behaviors, the functional purpose of this hidden map became clear. When a mouse performed a coordinated, multi-part action, such as raising both forepaws toward its mouth while simultaneously licking them, the corresponding forepaw, mouth, and tongue zones within the M2 map lit up together in intense, coordinated bursts.

Recent findings suggest that “All of these features of M2 explain why understanding the activity patterns of M2 has been so challenging,” remarked corresponding author Dr. Elizabeth Hillman, now chair of the Department of Imaging Sciences at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital. “Confusingly, M2 chatters when the body is still, and cares more about complicated movements than simple ones.”.

By revealing how M2 bridges sensory maps with multi-limb motor execution, the findings offer a foundational biological blueprint for understanding how the brain looks and updates complex actions from moment to moment.

“This newfound map could help researchers understand key details about the dextrous movements that can be lost after brain injuries such as strokes,” Xu noted, adding that decoding how resting-state cortical chatter reflects underlying structural wiring opens new avenues for assessing circuit integrity after neurological trauma.

Beyond clinical neurorehabilitation and movement disorders, deciphering how biological brains effortlessly synchronize dozens of joints and sensory streams provides an architectural template for engineers designing next-generation, dexterous autonomous robots.

How does the secondary motor cortex (M2) differ from the primary motor cortex (M1)?

The primary motor cortex (M1) sends direct signals down the spinal cord to control simple, isolated movements of individual body parts. In contrast, the secondary motor cortex (M2) specializes in orchestrating complex, coordinated movements that require multiple body parts to work together simultaneously, such as bringing a cup to your lips.

How did researchers discover the hidden body map in M2?

It has been revealed that instead of relying on traditional electrical stimulation, researchers used high-speed wide-field optical imaging to watch brain activity while mice were resting. They discovered small patches in M2 whose spontaneous resting activity synchronized with known body-part regions in the sensory cortex, forming a complete, previously undetected map.

Why is this discovery important for stroke recovery and robotics?

Recent findings suggest that understanding how M2 maps and coordinates multi-limb movements helps neuroscientists pinpoint why complex dexterity is lost after strokes or brain injuries, potentially guiding targeted neurorehabilitation. It also gives robotics engineers a biological blueprint for programming fluid, multi-joint coordination.

Recent findings suggest that funding: Funding for this work was provided by National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke BRAIN Initiative grants U19NS104649, R01 NS076628, R01 NS063226 and UM1NS132358 National Institute of Mental Health BRAIN Initiative grants RF1 MH114276 and RF1MH128969, the Simons Collaboration on the Global Brain grant 542991 and Foundation Leducq grant 22CVD01, and the American Lebanese Syrian Associated Charities (ALSAC), the fundraising and awareness organization of St. Jude.

Intrinsic Neural Dynamics Reveal a Body-Part-Specific Topography in Mouse Secondary Motor Cortex.

Recent findings suggest that the mammalian sensory cortex (S1) has a well-characterized body part-specific topography. However, most motor cortex atlases to date are only coarsely defined.

Here, we demonstrate that optical mapping of neuronal activity in awake mice reveals a distinct, body-part specific organization of mouse secondary motor cortex (M2).

It has been revealed that this M2 topography was identified by recognizing that intrinsic neuronal fluctuations are selectively synchronized between homologous sub-regions of S1 and M2. These fluctuations were strongest during rest and quenched during movement, and were not prominent in corticospinal neurons (CSNs), indicating that they do not represent motor output.

Functional characterization of M2 sub-regions during spontaneous movements confirms body-part specificity, and stronger engagement during multi-effector coordinated actions. Structural connectivity atlas tracings from S1 regions confirm projections to homologous M2 sub-regions.

These results reveal an key underlying topography within M2, and demonstrate intrinsic neuronal dynamics as a window into the functional architecture of the motor cortex.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With low miles, a six-speed stick, and nothing-rhymes-with-it upholstery, today's Nice Price or No Dice 350Z convertible has a lot going for it as a fun-time car.
  • It's been said—by old Shakespeare, no less—that beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
  • Sources indicate that when it comes to cars and trucks, value is rooted not only in price, but also in perceived usefulness and desirability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With low miles, a six-speed stick, and nothing-rhymes-with-it upholstery, today's Nice Price or No Dice 350Z convertible has a lot going for it as a fun-time car. Let's see how serious we feel about buying it at the seller's asking price.

It's been said—by old Shakespeare, no less—that beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Value, it should likewise be noted, is also a subjective concept. One person's fancy restaurant burger is another's meal budget for an entire week. Mmmm, ramen.

Sources indicate that when it comes to cars and trucks, value is rooted not only in price, but also in perceived usefulness and desirability. The seller of the 1999 Ford Expedition XLT that we looked at last Friday asked only $2,600 for it, a mere pittance in today's market. We had to consider, however, not just the dollars, but the desirability of a large SUV like that. Not everybody is keen on something that gets around 12 mpg around town and eyes compact parking spaces the same way Santa looks at skinny jeans. For many of you, that price was too hard to beat, regardless of potential pitfalls. The result was an overwhelming 89% 'Nice Price' win.

Recent findings suggest that have you looked at a weather report lately? According to meteorologists (which, by the way, is the coolest job title out there next to automotive journalist), North America is about to experience a wet and wild winter, thanks to the Super El Niño now taking up residence in the Pacific. Stormy weather? Wet, maybe slushy roads? That means this might not be the best time to consider buying a RWD, convertible sports car.

Being a community of naysayers, though, and those who forge our own path (usually sideways or backward, spraying a rooster tail of dirt and grass), that's just what we're going to consider. The object of our attention, this 2004 Nissan 350Z convertible, is sufficiently unique in a desirable way to warrant our immediate attention, even if using it to its full potential and driver enjoyment might have to wait until the drier days of Spring and Summer.

Industry observers note that okay, so what's to like about this 350Z? Well, for starters, it's a front-mid engine two-seater with a 287-horsepower naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V6 under the hood, mated to a six-speed manual. That's a spicy meatball right there. Then there's the convertible top. Yes, not everyone likes unlimited headroom and showing off a Rogaine prescription for all to see, but some do.

According to recent reports, as added enticements, the seller claims that the car is completely factory-stock and has a mere 61,000 miles on the clock. That's less than 3,000 miles a year. What a waste!

The reason given for the meager miles is that the car has been used exclusively as a weekend warrior for the past few years, sitting out the work week entirely. As a result, the car is stated to be in excellent condition, with a smooth-shifting gearbox and a fuss-free engine. With so few miles under its belt, we have to wonder if it's even on its original brake pads.

Another reason to check out this Z is its almost-latest appearance. Painted in dark silver metallic—as were, it seems, 90% of these cars—this Z looks clean and well-kept. The black fabric top is in equally good condition, as are the factory alloys. The tires wrapping those have plenty of tread depth but are cheap-seats Phantom HRX meats which, while not terrible, were probably chosen with the car's sale in mind.

This Z's party piece, however, is its two bucket seats. The rest of the cabin is dullsville black plastic, but the seats, cosseting, modestly-bolstered affairs, are orange-dyed leather with charcoal mesh insets. Those are in great shape, happily showing no wear whatsoever in the pictures. Equally up to snuff are the steering wheel wrap and shift knob, two more leather surfaces. The car has a full complement of comfort and convenience features—cruise, climate control, power windows and locks, etc.—and all are stated to work as they should. The cabin also has the added, odd benefit of a factory Bose stereo with both a CD and cassette player built right in.

So far, we've established that this Z puts a lot on the table for an enthusiast to enjoy. Two final incentives: it also has a clean title and the seller's insistence that this is a collectible model.

It has been revealed that known in America as the "Z" or "Z car," Nissan's venerated sports car carried the wonderful Fairlady name in its home market. Over the years, changing market priorities have stunted the Z's U.S. sales. While Nissan has dutifully stuck it out and still sells an updated version of this car today, when was the last time you saw one on the road? In fact, while the company has introduced the new 2027 models, its website still touts that "last year's model year Nissan Z is still available." How sad is that? Maybe the $45K price tag plays a role.

It has been revealed that this older, but claimed "like-upcoming" Z asks a far lower $12,500, and it's now time for you all to weigh in on whether that's a fair price or not. What do you think? Is this well-equipped, fantastically upholstered 350Z worth $12,500 as presented in its ad? Or does that price have you thinking about going Rogue?

#268. Mapping the Brain’s Energy Budget: How ATP Fuels Thought

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (846 w)
